1.title: She Unnames Them
1.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
1.why: Eve gives the animals' names back, and then her own. Without the names, the wall between her and the animals falls, and she finds that she must now speak slowly and with care. The story shows the passage's pair: the named world of the ten thousand things, and the nameless that was there before it. Le Guin later made her own English version of the Daodejing.

1.title: The Snow Man
1.creator: Wallace Stevens
1.why: A listener stands in a winter landscape and adds no feeling of their own to it. The poem asks for a mind that sees only what is there, and also the nothing that is there. This is close to the passage's 'always without wanting, to watch its fineness'. The wanting mind sees the edges of things; the still mind sees what is before the edges.

1.title: On Exactitude in Science
1.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
1.why: An empire makes a map as large as the land itself, point for point. The map is useless, and later generations leave it to rot in the desert. The one-paragraph story shows by contrast what the passage's first lines say: a way that is fully told, and a name that is fully given, are not the constant thing that they describe.

1.title: Arrival
1.creator: Denis Villeneuve
1.why: A linguist learns a written language of circles that has no before and after. As she learns its names, she starts to see time in a different way. The film can be read as a picture of 'Named: the mother of the ten thousand things': a naming system makes a world. The film also shows that something larger stays outside every such system.

2.title: The Left Hand of Darkness
2.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
2.why: An envoy visits a world where people are not fixed as male or female. He learns a local verse in which light and darkness are the two hands of one body, and he draws the yin-yang sign for his friend. The novel shows the passage's claim that the two sides of a pair give birth to each other. A person who keeps only one side misunderstands both.

2.title: Both Sides, Now
2.creator: Joni Mitchell (first recorded by Judy Collins)
2.why: The singer looks at clouds, at love, and at life, each from two opposite sides. She then says that she still does not know the thing itself. The song does not choose a winning side. It is close to the passage: the beautiful and the ugly arrive together, and a view from one side is only half of a pair.

2.title: Inside Out
2.creator: Pete Docter (Pixar)
2.why: Joy tries to keep Sadness away from a girl's memories, and the girl's inner world starts to break. The repair comes when Joy sees that the happy memories were made together with the sad ones. The film shows 'there, already, is the not-good' as a fact of the heart: the two sides complete each other, as hard and easy do.

2.title: Eye of the Beholder (The Twilight Zone)
2.creator: Rod Serling
2.why: Doctors try to repair a woman's face so that she looks like everyone else. At the end the viewer sees the faces, and the judgment of beautiful and ugly turns over. The episode shows the passage's first lines. When all under heaven agree on what is beautiful, that same agreement makes the ugly, and it makes an outcast.

3.title: The Gods Must Be Crazy
3.creator: Jamie Uys
3.why: A glass bottle falls from an aircraft into a Kalahari band that owns almost nothing. The bottle is useful, and there is only one. For the first time the people feel envy and anger. One man walks to the edge of the world to throw the bottle away. The comedy shows 'not prizing goods hard to get' with one object.

3.title: A Diamond Is Forever
3.creator: Frances Gerety, N. W. Ayer & Son, for De Beers
3.why: This advertising line taught several generations that a marriage needs a diamond. It made a stone into a good that is hard to get and that must be shown. It is the passage turned around: 'showing what can be desired' as a planned trade. The passage says that such showing puts the people's heart in disorder.

3.title: Harrison Bergeron
3.creator: Kurt Vonnegut
3.why: A future state makes all people equal by force. Strong people carry weights, and clever people hear loud noises that break their thoughts. The story is a warning about one reading of this passage. 'Not exalting the worthy' and 'weaken the will' become cruel when a clever ruler forces them. The passage ends with not-forcing.

3.title: The Lathe of Heaven
3.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
3.why: A quiet man has dreams that change the world. His doctor uses the dreams to repair the world: war, crowding, race. Each repair makes a worse problem. The doctor is one of the passage's 'clever ones' who dare to act. The dreamer wants only to stop forcing. Le Guin took the title from the Zhuangzi and several chapter mottoes from Daoist texts.

3.title: Mad Men
3.creator: Matthew Weiner
3.why: The series follows people in a 1960s advertising agency. Their work is to show what can be desired, and the best of them know that the want never ends. Their own lives show the cost: restless hearts in full houses. The series is a long picture of the opposite of 'empty the heart, fill the belly'.

4.title: Being There
4.creator: Hal Ashby; novel by Jerzy Kosinski
4.why: Chance is a gardener with no plans and no opinions. Powerful people meet him and hear deep advice in his plain words about plants. They pour their meaning into him, and he does not fill. The film is a comedy, and it also shows the passage's image: an empty bowl that people use again and again.

4.title: Columbo
4.creator: Richard Levinson and William Link
4.why: The detective wears an old raincoat, forgets his pencil, and praises the suspect's fine house. He blunts his own sharpness and tempers his own light, and proud people stop guarding themselves. Then he unties the knot. The series shows four lines of the passage as a working method: blunt, untie, temper, join the dust.

4.title: Spirited Away
4.creator: Hayao Miyazaki
4.why: No-Face is a spirit with a mask and nothing inside. In the greedy bathhouse he tries to fill the emptiness: he makes gold, eats food, and then eats workers, and he only gets larger and sadder. Away from the bathhouse he is quiet and useful. He shows the passage by contrast: an emptiness that people try to fill, and an emptiness that people leave open.

4.title: I'm Nobody! Who are you?
4.creator: Emily Dickinson
4.why: The speaker is glad to be nobody, and finds a second nobody to share the secret. To be somebody looks to her like a loud and public job. The short poem has the mood of 'tempering the light, joining the dust'. The passage's Dao is also hard to see: 'it seems, perhaps, to be there'.

5.title: Straw Dogs
5.creator: Sam Peckinpah
5.why: Peckinpah took the film's title from this passage. A mild scholar in an English village is pushed until he kills the men who attack his house. The film reads 'straw dogs' in a dark way: people are things to be used and thrown away. The passage itself says less than this. It says that heaven and earth do not take sides.

5.title: Straw Dogs: Thoughts on Humans and Other Animals
5.creator: John Gray
5.why: The philosopher John Gray takes his title from this passage. He argues that humans are one animal among the others, and that the world has no special plan for them. The book is a modern, sharp version of the first four lines: heaven and earth are not humane, and they do not treat people as an exception.

5.title: The Open Boat
5.creator: Stephen Crane
5.why: Four men from a sunk ship row a small boat toward the shore. One of them sees that the sea is not cruel and not kind. It does not see him at all. Then the men look after each other. The story shows 'heaven and earth are not humane' without despair: the sea treats all four men the same.

5.title: Grizzly Man
5.creator: Werner Herzog
5.why: Timothy Treadwell lived among Alaskan bears and believed that they knew and loved him. A bear killed him. Herzog, who made the film from Treadwell's own tapes, says that he sees in the bears' faces only a search for food. The film puts two views side by side, and Herzog's view is the passage's first line.

6.title: Princess Mononoke
6.creator: Hayao Miyazaki
6.why: Deep in a forest lives a spirit that gives life and takes life with each step. People cut off its head to own its power, and the land starts to die. When the head is returned, green comes back over the burned hills. The film shows a source that is used and does not wear out, and that does not die.

6.title: Always Coming Home
6.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
6.why: The book collects the songs, stories, and customs of a people who live in a place that they call the Valley. They do not conquer and they do not build empires. Descent runs through the mother's house. The book can be read as a long picture of a culture built on the passage's images: the valley and the female root.

6.title: The force that through the green fuse drives the flower
6.creator: Dylan Thomas
6.why: One hidden force pushes the flower up, moves the water, and moves the speaker's own blood. The same force also brings each of them to an end. The poem does not name the force. It is near to the passage's thin thread that 'seems to be there', the root from which all things come, and which use does not exhaust.

6.title: Moana
6.creator: Ron Clements and John Musker (Disney)
6.why: An island goddess is the source of all life in the sea. A hero steals her heart to give its power to people, and a slow rot spreads from island to island. A girl returns the heart, and life returns. The film shows the 'root of heaven and earth' as female, quiet, and generous. It also shows the cost when people try to own the root.

7.title: It's a Wonderful Life
7.creator: Frank Capra
7.why: George Bailey gives up his travels, his college, and his own plans, each time for other people. He thinks that he has put his life behind him and lost it. On one night the whole town comes to carry him. The film shows the passage's turn: he 'puts the body behind, and the body is in front'.

7.title: Ikiru
7.creator: Akira Kurosawa
7.why: A city clerk learns that he will soon die. He spends his last months pushing one small playground through the offices, and he takes no credit. After his death other men claim the work. The people of the district know who did it. He is 'without the private', and so the one thing that was his own is completed.

7.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
7.creator: Oscar Wilde
7.why: A young man wishes that his portrait will grow old in his place. He then lives only for his own pleasure and his own face. He keeps his body and loses everything else, and at the end he loses the body too. The novel is the opposite path to the passage: he lives for himself, and so he does not last.

7.title: Groundhog Day
7.creator: Harold Ramis
7.why: A proud weatherman must live the same day again and again. First he uses the day for himself, and it does not end. Later he spends each day on the people of the town and asks for nothing. Only then does the next morning come. The film shows that the private is completed when a person stops living for the private.

8.title: Longstreet
8.creator: Stirling Silliphant (with Bruce Lee)
8.why: Bruce Lee plays a martial-arts teacher in this detective series. He tells his blind student to be without a fixed form, like water, which takes the shape of any cup. Lee repeated the idea in a 1971 television interview with Pierre Berton. The lesson is the passage in a fight: water does not contend, and so nothing can block it.

8.title: Bitter Work (Avatar: The Last Airbender)
8.creator: Aaron Ehasz (writer); Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko (series creators)
8.why: Iroh teaches his nephew to turn lightning aside. He learned the method by watching waterbenders: do not block the force, but give it a path through the body and out. Zuko's own anger is what keeps him from making lightning. The episode shows water as a teacher of those who use force.

8.title: Bridge over Troubled Water
8.creator: Simon & Garfunkel (written by Paul Simon)
8.why: The singer offers to go down low so that a tired friend can cross over. The singer asks for nothing and does not compete for notice. The song takes the passage's side of the high and low pair. Its help comes from the low place, as water benefits the ten thousand things 'in the place the crowd hates'.

8.title: Siddhartha
8.creator: Hermann Hesse
8.why: After years as a monk and then as a rich merchant, Siddhartha becomes a ferryman's helper. The old ferryman has a low station and few words, and he has learned all that he knows from the river. Siddhartha learns to listen to the water too. The novel shows the passage's claim that the low place is near to Dao.

8.title: There Will Be Blood
8.creator: Paul Thomas Anderson
8.why: An oil man says that he has a competition in him and that he wants no one else to succeed. He takes what is under other people's land and wins every contest. He ends alone in a large house, with a dead man on the floor. The film shows the cost of the opposite of water: contending in all things.

9.title: Citizen Kane
9.creator: Orson Welles
9.why: Kane fills a palace with statues and goods from all over the world. Many of them stay in their boxes. He dies alone there, and workers burn the things that nobody wants. The film is a full picture of two lines of the passage: 'Gold and jade fill the hall: no one can guard them.'

9.title: Ozymandias
9.creator: Percy Bysshe Shelley
9.why: A traveller finds two stone legs and a broken face in an empty desert. The words on the base tell the mighty to look at the king's works and despair. No works are left. The poem shows the passage's line on those who are 'rich, high in rank, and proud': the pride itself carries the ruin.

9.title: Breaking Bad
9.creator: Vince Gilligan
9.why: A teacher starts to make drugs to leave money for his family. He soon has more than they can ever spend, and he does not stop, because he wants to be the best at it. The pile of money in a storage room is the passage's vessel filled to the brim. 'Better to have stopped' is the whole story.

9.title: One Last Time (Hamilton)
9.creator: Lin-Manuel Miranda
9.why: George Washington tells Hamilton that he will not seek another term. He wants the country to learn how to go on without him. Hamilton argues, and then he writes the farewell. The song shows the passage's last lines as a public act: 'The work carried through, the body steps back.'

9.title: The Great Gatsby
9.creator: F. Scott Fitzgerald
9.why: Gatsby builds a great house, fills it with guests and shirts and music, and holds it up as an offer to one woman. He cannot stop at enough, because the display is the point. When he dies, almost no guest comes to the funeral. The novel shows a hall filled with gold and jade that no one guards.

10.title: Kung Fu Panda
10.creator: Mark Osborne and John Stevenson (DreamWorks)
10.why: A soft, round panda is chosen over five hard fighters. The secret scroll that all of them want is a blank, shining surface that shows the reader's own face. The old tortoise master tells the teacher to stop controlling. The film plays with several of the passage's questions: softness like an infant, a clear mirror, and raising without ruling.

10.title: The Prophet
10.creator: Kahlil Gibran
10.why: In the part about children, the prophet tells parents that their children come through them and do not belong to them. Parents can give love and a house, but not their own thoughts. He compares the parent to a bow and the child to an arrow. This is the passage's 'giving life, not owning; raising, not ruling' in a much-loved modern form.

10.title: Finding Nemo
10.creator: Andrew Stanton (Pixar)
10.why: A father fish has lost almost all his family, and he holds his last son so tightly that the son swims away to prove himself. The father crosses the sea to find him. At the end the father must let the son go into danger and trust him. The film is one long answer to 'raising, not ruling'.

10.title: If You Love Somebody Set Them Free
10.creator: Sting
10.why: The song says that love is not possession, and that a person cannot keep another person like a thing in a box. Sting wrote it partly as an answer to his own earlier hit about watching a lover. Its plain message is the passage's 'giving life, not owning', moved from the parent and the ruler to the lover.

11.creator: John Cage
11.why: A player sits at the instrument for three movements and plays no note. The piece is a frame with nothing in it, and the room fills it: rain, coughs, chairs, breath. Cage was drawing on Zen Buddhism and the Chinese I Ching at the time. The piece does for music what the passage does for the wheel: the use is 'right at its nothing'.

11.title: Think Small
11.creator: Doyle Dane Bernbach (Helmut Krone, Julian Koenig), for Volkswagen
11.why: A very small picture of a car sits on a page that is almost all white space. Other car advertisements of the time filled every corner. This one made readers stop and look, and it changed the trade. The empty paper does the work. It is the passage's clay vessel in print: the gain is in what is there, and the use is in what is not.

11.title: Portal
11.creator: Valve
11.why: The player has one tool, and the tool makes holes. Every wall, floor, and gap in the test rooms is solved by an opening, not by a thing. The player learns to see a room by its empty places. The game is a modern exercise in the passage's third image: 'Cut doors and windows to make a room.'

11.title: Late Spring
11.creator: Yasujirō Ozu
11.why: A daughter must marry and leave her father. On their last trip, at night, the camera leaves her face and rests on a vase in a dim room. Nothing happens in the shot. Viewers have argued about it for decades, because the empty shot holds the feeling of the whole film. The nothing gives the use.

11.title: Hills Like White Elephants
11.creator: Ernest Hemingway
11.why: A man and a young woman wait for a train and talk about drinks and hills. They never name the thing that they are deciding. The story is built around that hole, as a wheel is built around its hub. The reader feels the weight because of what is absent from the page.

12.title: Fifteen Million Merits (Black Mirror)
12.creator: Charlie Brooker and Konnie Huq
12.why: People live in small rooms whose walls are screens. They ride exercise bicycles to earn credits, and they must pay to skip the advertisements. When one man shouts the truth on a talent show, his anger becomes a new programme. The episode shows the five colors and the five notes at full strength, and the blind eye and deaf ear that result.

12.title: WALL-E
12.creator: Andrew Stanton (Pixar)
12.why: On a starship, people float in chairs with a screen in front of each face and a drink in each hand. They have not seen the pool beside them or the person next to them. A small robot knocks one screen away, and a woman looks up. The film shows the passage's eye that is blind from too much colour.

12.title: Infinite Jest
12.creator: David Foster Wallace
12.why: At the centre of this long novel is a film that is so pleasing that viewers cannot stop watching, and they die in front of it. Around it are people caught by drugs, sport, and television. The novel takes the passage's warning to its limit: what feeds only the eye can make the heart 'break out in madness'.

12.title: (I Can't Get No) Satisfaction
12.creator: The Rolling Stones
12.why: The singer hears a radio voice and a television man who tell him what to want and how his shirts must look. He tries and tries, and no satisfaction comes. The song is a complaint from inside the world of the passage's first five lines. More notes and more colours leave the ear and eye more hungry.

12.title: Walden
12.creator: Henry David Thoreau
12.why: Thoreau lives for two years in a small house that he built beside a pond. He counts the cost of his beans and his nails, and he asks what a person needs. He drops the rest as weight. The book is an American trial of 'for the belly, not for the eye': he leaves that and takes this.

13.title: Nosedive (Black Mirror)
13.creator: Charlie Brooker, Rashida Jones, Michael Schur; directed by Joe Wright
13.why: Every meeting ends with a score from one to five, and the score decides a person's house, seat, and friends. A woman with a good score lives in fear of each small look, and then she falls. The episode shows the passage's first line in full: getting favor startles her, and losing favor startles her.

13.title: Sunset Boulevard
13.creator: Billy Wilder
13.why: A star of silent films lives in a decaying house with her old pictures. She waits for the public's love to return. Favor once made her great, and so she could not live when it left. The film shows why the passage says that 'favor makes the lower one': the one who receives favor depends on the one who gives it.

13.title: BoJack Horseman
13.creator: Raphael Bob-Waksberg
13.why: A former television star wins new praise, a mistaken Oscar nomination, and a new series. None of it calms him, and each loss of praise breaks him again. The series is a long study of the self that favor and disgrace both startle. It is the 'great trouble' that the passage ties to having a self to defend.

13.title: If—
13.creator: Rudyard Kipling
13.why: A father lists for his son the marks of a steady person. One line is the passage in small: to meet Triumph and Disaster 'and treat those two impostors just the same'. Kipling asks for a stiff will. The passage goes one step further: it says that favor and disgrace are equally a start of fear.

14.title: Mushishi
14.creator: Yuki Urushibara
14.why: Ginko walks from village to village and studies mushi: forms of life near the source of all life, which most people cannot see, hear, or hold. He does not kill them when he can avoid it. He learns how they move and helps people live beside them. The series gives a quiet picture of 'the shape of no shape'.

14.title: Star Wars
14.creator: George Lucas
14.why: An old teacher tells a farm boy about a field that surrounds and joins all living things. The boy cannot see it. He hits the target only when he switches off his targeting computer and trusts the Force. Writers have often compared the Force with Daoist ideas of Dao and qi. The scene fits 'looked at, not seen'.

14.title: Solaris
14.creator: Stanisław Lem
14.why: Scientists have studied a living ocean on a far planet for a hundred years. They have filled libraries with names and theories, and they still do not know what it is or if it knows them. The novel is a long form of one line of the passage: these things 'cannot be questioned to the end'.

14.title: The Little Prince
14.creator: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
14.why: A fox teaches a small prince a secret about the things that matter most: the eye cannot see them. The pilot who tells the story learns that a desert is beautiful because a well is hidden in it. The book gives children the passage's first claim, that the real thing is looked at and not seen.

15.title: Mister Rogers' Neighborhood
15.creator: Fred Rogers
15.why: Fred Rogers changes his shoes slowly, feeds the fish, and lets a long silence stay in the programme. He does not hurry a child's question. Television around him became louder and faster for thirty years, and he did not. The programme shows the passage's question about muddy water that comes clear slowly, through stillness.

15.title: Kiki's Delivery Service
15.creator: Hayao Miyazaki
15.why: A young witch works hard at her delivery job and then loses the power to fly. A painter friend tells her about her own blocks: she stops trying, walks, sleeps, and waits. Kiki rests, and the power returns when it is needed. The film shows both of the passage's questions: stillness that clears, and movement that brings back life.

15.title: Seven Samurai
15.creator: Akira Kurosawa
15.why: The leader of the seven is an old soldier who has lost many battles. He is watchful at every door, plain in his manner, and slow to speak. The best swordsman of the group is the quietest man in it. The film gives faces to the passage's list: 'wary, as if crossing a river in winter'.

15.title: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
15.creator: Robert M. Pirsig
15.why: The narrator describes the moment when a mechanic is stuck on a screw that will not turn. He says that the stuck moment is not a failure. The mechanic must stop, look at the machine with no plan, and wait for the mind to settle. This is the passage's muddy water, cleared through stillness, in a workshop.

16.title: Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring
16.creator: Kim Ki-duk
16.why: A small temple floats on a lake. A boy grows up there, leaves in passion, returns in guilt, becomes the old monk, and receives a new boy. Each season of the film is one age of his life. The film is Buddhist, and it shows the passage's line with great calm: things 'each go home again to the root'.

16.title: Turn! Turn! Turn!
16.creator: Pete Seeger; recorded by The Byrds
16.why: Seeger set to music the list of paired seasons from the book of Ecclesiastes: a time to be born and a time to die, to plant and to pull up. The Byrds made it a hit. The song watches things rise and go back, as the passage does, and it does not call one half of each pair good.

16.title: Four Quartets
16.creator: T. S. Eliot
16.why: Across four long poems Eliot looks for a still point in the middle of the turning world. He ends with the thought that all our searching will bring us back to the place where we started, and that we will know it for the first time. The poems are Christian. Their shape is the passage's: emptiness, stillness, and return.

16.title: Outer Wilds
16.creator: Mobius Digital
16.why: The player explores a small solar system for twenty-two minutes. Then the sun dies, and the same morning starts again. Nothing can stop the ending. The player can only watch, learn, and at last accept it beside a camp fire. The game teaches the passage's skill: 'I, by this, watch the return.'

16.title: The Lion King
16.creator: Roger Allers and Rob Minkoff (Disney)
16.why: A father shows his son that lions eat the antelope, and that dead lions become the grass that the antelope eat. The son runs from his place in this circle, and the land goes grey under a ruler who only takes. The land turns green when the son returns. The film shows return to the root, and the 'wild rising' of those who do not know it.

17.title: The Man Who Planted Trees
17.creator: Jean Giono
17.why: A shepherd plants one hundred acorns each day in a dry, empty valley. He does this for decades and tells nobody. Water returns, and then villages and families. Officials come to protect what they call a natural forest. This is the passage's last line almost word for word: the people say that it happened of itself.

17.title: Mary Poppins
17.creator: Robert Stevenson (Disney); books by P. L. Travers
17.why: A nanny arrives in an unhappy house. She gives few orders and no reasons. By the end the father has mended a kite and taken his children to the park, and he believes that the change is his own. The family does not see her leave. She is the passage's highest kind of leader: the work is done, and she is not in it.

17.title: 12 Angry Men
17.creator: Sidney Lumet; written by Reginald Rose
17.why: Eleven jurors vote guilty. The twelfth does not say that the accused is innocent. He asks questions, and he lets each man find his own doubt. At the end the jurors go their own ways, and almost no names are known. The film shows leading with few and costly words, so that each person says: I came to this myself.

17.title: Nineteen Eighty-Four
17.creator: George Orwell
17.why: The ruler's face is on every wall, and his screens watch every room. The state trusts no one, and so no one can trust the state or each other. The novel shows the third rank in the passage's list, the ruler whom people fear. It also shows the two lines on trust: where trust is not given, there is none.

18.title: The Remains of the Day
18.creator: Kazuo Ishiguro
18.why: An English butler has given his whole life to perfect, loyal service. His lord was a friend to the Nazis in the 1930s, and the butler did not let himself see it. His loyalty is real, and it is also a sign that the house had gone wrong. The novel shows the passage's last pair: a dark house, and a loyal minister.

18.title: The Handmaid's Tale
18.creator: Margaret Atwood
18.why: A new state speaks all day about virtue, duty, and family. It has fixed greetings, uniforms, and public prayers. Behind the words the leaders break their own rules. The novel shows the passage's second pair: when cleverness comes out, there is 'the great fabrication'. Loud right conduct is a sign that the Way is lost.

18.title: Succession
18.creator: Jesse Armstrong
18.why: Four adult children compete for their father's company. They say 'I love you' and 'family first' most often when they are about to betray each other. The series shows the passage's third pair. When the six kin are out of tune, speeches about devoted children and tender parents appear. In a family that is in tune, nobody needs the speeches.

18.title: The Dark Knight
18.creator: Christopher Nolan
18.why: A city's courts and police have failed. So the city has a masked hero, and it puts its hope in a brave prosecutor. The film is honest about this: a city that needs such men is a sick city, and the hero wants a day when he is not needed. This is the passage's logic of the loyal minister in a disordered state.

19.title: The Tao of Pooh
19.creator: Benjamin Hoff
19.why: Hoff uses A. A. Milne's bear to explain Daoist ideas to Western readers. Pooh is his example of pu, the uncarved wood: plain, not clever, and for that reason able to do what Rabbit and Owl cannot. The book is a direct, popular reading of this passage's last lines, and many readers first met the Daodejing through it.

19.title: Simple Gifts
19.creator: Joseph Brackett (Shaker song)
19.why: This Shaker dance song begins: 'Tis the gift to be simple, 'tis the gift to be free'. It says that a person who has come down to the right place will not be ashamed to bow and to bend. Aaron Copland later used the tune. The song shares the passage's trust in the undyed and the uncarved.

19.title: Perfect Days
19.creator: Wim Wenders
19.why: A man in Tokyo cleans public toilets with great care. He owns a few cassettes, some paperbacks, and some young trees. He photographs the light in the leaves at lunch. The film watches his days and does not explain him. It is a modern picture of 'less of what is private, fewer wants', with its sadness left in.

19.title: Fight Club
19.creator: David Fincher; novel by Chuck Palahniuk
19.why: An office worker hates his furniture catalogue life. He and a new friend throw away comfort and profit, and men follow them. The plain life soon becomes rules, uniforms, a leader, and bombs. The film is a warning about this passage read with force: 'cut off' and 'throw away' become a new cleverness, with no uncarved wood to fasten to.

20.title: The Big Lebowski
20.creator: Joel and Ethan Coen
20.why: The Dude has no job, no plan, and a dressing gown. The men around him are sharp and busy: a rich man, a soldier, artists, criminals. All of them have a use. He drifts through their plots, 'swaying, like the sea', and at the end he is the only one who is unchanged. The film is a comic portrait of the passage's speaker.

20.title: Bartleby, the Scrivener
20.creator: Herman Melville
20.why: A clerk in a Wall Street office answers each request with the words 'I would prefer not to'. He does not argue, and he does not leave. The busy lawyers cannot place him or use him. Bartleby is a darker brother of the passage's speaker: 'I alone am a block', alone among people who all have their use.

20.title: I Just Wasn't Made for These Times
20.creator: The Beach Boys (Brian Wilson and Tony Asher)
20.why: The singer looks for a place where he fits and for people who will stay with his ideas, and he does not find them. The music is rich, and the voice is alone in it. The song has the passage's central feeling: the crowd is merry and has more than enough, and 'I alone seem to have lost it'.

20.title: (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay
20.creator: Otis Redding and Steve Cropper
20.why: A man has left his home and crossed the country. He sits at the water and watches the ships and the tide. He will not do what people tell him to do, and nothing changes. The song stays in the passage's mood of drift and adds no moral: 'drooping, as with no home to go to'.

20.title: Lost in Translation
20.creator: Sofia Coppola
20.why: Two Americans cannot sleep in a Tokyo hotel. Around them are parties, game halls, and bright signs, and they feel no part of it. The film does not cure them. It lets them be dim together for a few days. It shows the passage's contrast between the bright, sharp crowd and the one who is 'dusk, dusk'.

21.title: Stalker
21.creator: Andrei Tarkovsky
21.why: A guide leads two men into a closed Zone. It is wet, green, and unclear, and no straight path is safe in it. The men are told that a room at the centre gives a person's deepest wish. The film never proves it. It shows the passage's claim: within the dim and flickering there is something very real. The guide also speaks a prayer that follows the Daodejing on softness.

21.title: Tomorrow Never Knows
21.creator: The Beatles (Lennon–McCartney)
21.why: John Lennon took the words from a 1964 guide to psychedelic experience that was based on the Tibetan Book of the Dead. The song tells the listener to stop thinking and float into a shining emptiness. One drone, tape loops, and a far voice make the sound itself dim and flickering. Within it, the song says, there is something to know.

21.title: Close Encounters of the Third Kind
21.creator: Steven Spielberg
21.why: After a light passes over his truck, a man has a shape in his mind that he cannot name. He builds it from shaving foam, potatoes, and mud. His family thinks that he is ill. The shape is a real mountain. The film is a story of the passage's sequence: first dim, then an image, then a thing, then a proof.

21.title: Blowup
21.creator: Michelangelo Antonioni
21.why: A photographer enlarges a picture of a park and thinks that he sees a body in the leaves. He enlarges again, and the image becomes grain. The film leaves the question open. It explores the same ground as the passage, from the side of doubt: how a person knows that 'within it there is a thing' when the image is only flickering.

22.title: Anthem
22.creator: Leonard Cohen
22.why: Cohen tells the listener to stop waiting for a perfect offering. In the song's best-known image, every thing has a break in it, and the break is where the light enters. The song does not praise damage and does not hide it. It joins the two sides, as the passage does: 'Bent, then whole.' 'Hollow, then full.'

22.title: The Velveteen Rabbit
22.creator: Margery Williams
22.why: An old toy horse explains to a new toy rabbit how a toy becomes Real. It happens slowly, when a child loves the toy for a long time. By then the fur is rubbed off and the joints are loose. The story is the passage's fourth line told for children: 'Worn, then new.'

22.title: Little Miss Sunshine
22.creator: Jonathan Dayton and Valerie Faris
22.why: A family of people who have each failed drives a broken van to a child beauty contest. The father sells a plan for winners. They lose the contest badly, on a stage, together, and they drive home whole for the first time. The film shows the passage's turn: when they stop contending, nobody can defeat them.

22.title: Celeste
22.creator: Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry (Maddy Makes Games)
22.why: A young woman climbs a mountain, and a dark copy of herself tries to stop her. She fights the copy, and she falls to the bottom. She climbs again only after she stops the fight and takes that part of herself with her. The game makes the player feel 'crooked, then straight' in the hands.

23.title: All Things Must Pass
23.creator: George Harrison
23.why: Harrison's song says that a sunrise does not last all morning and a cloudburst does not last all day. He took these images from Timothy Leary's poem version of this passage of the Daodejing, as Harrison himself said. The song is this passage in popular music: hard weather passes of itself, and so does grief.

23.title: Nothing Gold Can Stay
23.creator: Robert Frost
23.why: In eight short lines Frost says that the first green of spring is gold, and that it holds for only an hour. Leaf follows leaf, and dawn goes down to day. The poem has the passage's sparse words and its plain law. If heaven and earth cannot keep a high moment up, a person cannot.

23.title: The Red Turtle
23.creator: Michaël Dudok de Wit
23.why: A man is thrown onto an empty island. He fights it and tries three times to escape. Then he stops, and he lives a whole life there. A great wave destroys the forest, and the forest grows again. The film has no spoken words. It shows 'sparse words: so of itself', and a man who becomes one with his place.

23.title: Uncut Gems
23.creator: Josh and Benny Safdie
23.why: A New York jeweller bets, borrows, and talks without stopping for two hours of film. Each win is put on a larger bet. He tries to keep a whirlwind going for the whole day. The film shows by contrast the passage's weather: if even heaven and earth cannot keep a squall up, a man cannot.

24.title: The Emperor's New Clothes
24.creator: Hans Christian Andersen
24.why: An emperor loves fine dress and loves to be seen in it. Two cheats sell him cloth that does not exist, and he walks through the town in nothing. A child says so. The tale is the passage's third line in one picture: 'One who shows the self is not bright.' The show hides nothing, and all people see it.

24.title: You're So Vain
24.creator: Carly Simon
24.why: The singer describes a man who walks into a party as if he is boarding a yacht, and who watches himself in the mirror while he dances. He will also believe that this song is about him. The song is a light picture of the passage's self-display, and of why other people 'loathe' it.

24.title: The Office (UK)
24.creator: Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant
24.why: A paper company manager tells a camera crew that he is a great leader, a comedian, and a friend to his staff. The staff look at the floor. The more he praises himself, the less merit anyone sees. The series is the passage's middle lines made into comedy: 'One who boasts has no merit.'

24.title: Black Swan
24.creator: Darren Aronofsky
24.why: A ballet dancer wants to be perfect in a double role. She pushes her body and mind past what they can hold, and she breaks on the night of her triumph. The film shows the passage's first line as a life: a person can go up on tiptoe for one moment, but cannot stand there.

24.title: One-Punch Man
24.creator: ONE; redrawn by Yusuke Murata
24.why: Saitama can defeat any enemy with one hit. He has a low hero rank, a cheap apartment, and almost no fame, and he lets other heroes take the credit. Around him, heroes fight for rank and for a good image. The comedy puts the passage's two kinds side by side: the one who shows the self, and the one who does not.

25.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
25.creator: Stanley Kubrick
25.why: A black slab appears before humans exist, and the film never says what it is. Kubrick gives it no name and almost no words. A man follows it farther than anyone has gone, and he comes back toward the earth as a child. The film's shape is the passage's: great, passing on, far, and 'far means turning back'.

25.title: The Last Question
25.creator: Isaac Asimov
25.why: Across billions of years, people ask a growing computer whether the running-down of the universe can be reversed. The stars go out. People merge with the machine. At the far end of everything, the answer comes, and it is a beginning. The story can be read with the passage's line that what goes far turns back.

25.title: Phoenix
25.creator: Osamu Tezuka
25.why: Tezuka's life work jumps between Japan's far past and the far future, and each book moves closer to the present. An undying bird watches people grasp at long life, die, and come back in new forms. In one book all life ends and slowly starts again. The series shows something that 'goes all round and is not in danger'.

25.title: Everything
25.creator: David OReilly
25.why: The player can become any thing in the game: a bear, a stone, a galaxy, a grain of pollen. The player moves up and down in scale, and the largest level leads back into the smallest. Recorded talks by Alan Watts play during the game. It lets the player try the passage's chain: person, earth, heaven, Dao.

25.title: The Tree of Life
25.creator: Terrence Malick
25.why: The film puts one Texas family of the 1950s next to the birth of stars, seas, and the first animals. A mother's whispered questions go out to something that she cannot name. The film does not rank the small story below the large one. Like the passage, it sets the person, the earth, and heaven in one line.

26.title: The Unbearable Lightness of Being
26.creator: Milan Kundera
26.why: The novel opens with a question about the pair of weight and lightness: which one is good? One man keeps his loves light and free. One woman carries hers as a heavy fate. Kundera shows the cost and the gift of each side. The book is a modern study of the passage's first line: 'Heavy is the root of light.'

26.title: The Lord of the Rings
26.creator: J. R. R. Tolkien
26.why: Sam Gamgee carries the pack: the rope, the salt, and the cooking pots, almost to the mountain. He is slow, plain, and steady, and the quest fails without him. Frodo has the great task, and Sam is its root. Tolkien gives a face to the passage's traveller who 'does not leave the baggage wagons'.

26.title: Marie Antoinette
26.creator: Sofia Coppola
26.why: A young queen fills her days at Versailles with cakes, shoes, cards, and parties. The film stays inside the bright rooms with her, and the hungry country is far away, until a crowd is at the gate. It shows the passage's warning to the lord who is light before all under heaven: 'the root is lost'.

26.title: Like a Rolling Stone
26.creator: Bob Dylan
26.why: The singer speaks to a woman who was rich and well taught, and who laughed at people below her. Now she has no home and no direction, and she must deal with people whom she did not see before. The song asks her how that feels. It is the passage's last pair: light, and the root is lost.

26.title: Death Stranding
26.creator: Hideo Kojima (Kojima Productions)
26.why: The player is a porter who walks across a broken country with cargo on his back. The whole game is the load: how to stack it, balance it, and keep it dry. A player who runs light and fast falls. The game lets a person feel the passage's first line in the body: the heavy is the root of the light.

27.title: The Gleaners and I
27.creator: Agnès Varda
27.why: Varda films people who pick up what others leave: potatoes after the harvest, food from market bins, broken clocks and dolls. Some do it from need and some from choice. She films her own old hands too, as one more found thing. The documentary shows the passage's promise: 'there is no discarded thing', and no discarded person.

27.title: Les Misérables
27.creator: Victor Hugo
27.why: A bishop gives a bed to a released convict whom every inn has refused. The convict steals his silver. When the police bring the man back, the bishop says that the silver was a gift and adds two candlesticks. The man's whole later life grows from this. The bishop is 'good at coming to people's aid', and so no person is discarded.

27.title: Lilo & Stitch
27.creator: Chris Sanders and Dean DeBlois (Disney)
27.why: Stitch is a failed experiment that was made to destroy, and his makers want to lock him away. Lilo is a lonely girl whom the other children avoid. Her small, broken family takes him in, with the rule that nobody is left behind. The film shows the passage from the side of those whom others discard.

27.title: Good Will Hunting
27.creator: Gus Van Sant; written by Matt Damon and Ben Affleck
27.why: A cleaner at a university is a mathematical genius, and he hits people and pushes help away. Five therapists give up. The sixth stays, and the work with the young man also opens the therapist's own closed grief. The film shows the passage's pair: the teacher and the material need each other, and each must be prized.

27.title: Shoplifters
27.creator: Hirokazu Kore-eda
27.why: A poor group in Tokyo lives as a family. No one in it is related by law: an old woman, a couple, a runaway, a boy, and a small girl whom they find cold on a balcony. Each of them was left by someone. The film asks who is skilled at keeping people, and it complicates the passage's 'no discarded person'.

28.title: The Left Hand of Darkness
28.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
28.why: The people of the planet Gethen are male and female in one body, by turns. The envoy from Earth must drop his habit of ranking the two sides. The novel shows the first pair of this passage: know the cock, keep to the hen. Le Guin later made her own English version of the Tao Te Ching, and the book uses light and shadow as a second pair.

28.title: Orlando: A Biography
28.creator: Virginia Woolf
28.why: Orlando lives for centuries, first as a man and then as a woman, and stays one person. The change takes nothing away. Orlando knows the male side from inside and then keeps to the female side. The book can be read as a picture of holding both sides of the first pair, with no side made the lesser.

28.title: The Little Prince
28.creator: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
28.why: A pilot who has learned the adult world of numbers and rank meets a child who sees plain things as they are. The pilot does not forget what he knows. He goes back to the child's sight and keeps it. This is the movement the passage names three times: know the high side, keep to the low side, and go back again to the infant.

28.title: Fight Club
28.creator: David Fincher (film); Chuck Palahniuk (novel)
28.why: Men who feel small build a club and then an army on hardness only. They know the cock and throw the hen away. The result is not strength. The result is a mind split in two and a city in danger. The film shows the cost of holding one side of the pair and refusing the other.

29.title: The Lathe of Heaven
29.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
29.why: George Orr's dreams change the real world. His doctor uses the dreams to repair the world: no war, no hunger, no crowding. Each repair brings a worse harm. This is the passage as a story: the world is a spirit vessel, and who works on it ruins it. Le Guin took the title from the Zhuangzi and put Daoist lines at the head of chapters.

29.title: The Lord of the Rings
29.creator: J. R. R. Tolkien
29.why: The Ring gives the power to order the whole world. Every strong person who grips the Ring is ruined by it, even those who want to do good. The wise refuse to take the Ring at all. The story shows the two lines at the center of the passage: who works on it ruins it, and who grips it loses it.

29.title: Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind
29.creator: Hayao Miyazaki
29.why: Kingdoms want to burn a poison forest and take control of the land. Nausicaä learns that the forest is cleaning the earth by its own slow process. The people who try to fix the world by force bring disaster. She watches, follows, and does not grip. The film shows a world that cannot be worked on.

29.title: Jurassic Park
29.creator: Steven Spielberg (film); Michael Crichton (novel)
29.why: A rich man makes a living world and believes he can manage every part of it with fences and computers. The creatures do not stay in the plan. Some go ahead and some follow, as the passage says of all creatures. The park fails in one night. The grand plan is the thing that the sage puts away.

29.title: Everybody Wants to Rule the World
29.creator: Tears for Fears
29.why: The song names the common wish to take the world and hold it. The bright tune carries a warning: the control does not last, and the wish itself wears people down. It gives the mood of the first line of the passage, the wanting to take all under heaven, and it shows why the sage puts the grand away.

30.title: Ozymandias
30.creator: Percy Bysshe Shelley
30.why: A traveller finds the broken statue of a king who boasted of his works. The boast is still cut in the stone, and sand is all around. Shelley's line is short: "Nothing beside remains." The poem shows the last line of the passage. A creature at full strength then grows old, and force that took the strong place does not keep it.

30.title: Grave of the Fireflies
30.creator: Isao Takahata (film); Akiyuki Nosaka (story)
30.why: Two children try to stay alive in Japan in the last months of the war. No battle is on screen for long. The film shows what comes after the armies: burned towns and no food. It is the passage's own image. Where an army has camped, thorns grow, and after a great host there are years of hunger.

30.title: Where Have All the Flowers Gone?
30.creator: Pete Seeger and Joe Hickerson
30.why: The song moves in a circle: flowers, young women, young men, soldiers, graves, and flowers again. Each verse asks the same question of the next thing; Joe Hickerson's later verses, added in 1960, close the circle. War is not shown as an event that ends. War is shown as business that comes back, which is the third line of the passage.

30.title: Seven Samurai
30.creator: Akira Kurosawa
30.why: Farmers hire seven fighters to stop a band of robbers. The fighters do the work because there is no other choice, and four of them die. At the end the farmers sing and plant rice. The leader says that the victory belongs to the farmers. The film shows fruit, and stop: the result, with no pride and no strong place taken.

30.title: Munich
30.creator: Steven Spielberg
30.why: A team is sent to kill the men behind an attack. Each killing is answered by a new killing, and new men take the place of the dead. The leader ends with fear and no rest. The film shows the line that such business likes to come back. Force does not stop at its fruit here, and so it has no end.

31.title: All Quiet on the Western Front
31.creator: Erich Maria Remarque
31.why: A German schoolboy goes to the trenches with his class, and the class dies around him. The teachers at home speak of glory. The soldiers see only the dead. The novel treats every battle as a funeral, for both sides. That is the rule of the passage: mourn the many killed, and hold the victory with the rites of grief.

31.title: Dulce et Decorum est
31.creator: Wilfred Owen
31.why: Owen describes a gas attack and one man who does not get his mask on in time. Then he turns to the people at home who call death in war sweet and fitting. He calls that saying a lie. The poem is the passage's warning in a soldier's voice: do not find victory beautiful.

31.title: Unforgiven
31.creator: Clint Eastwood
31.why: An old gunman takes one more job. A young man who admired killers kills for the first time and is sick with it. The old man tells him plainly how heavy a killing is. The Western usually finds the gun beautiful. This film refuses to. It shows weapons as tools of ill omen, used with no delight.

31.title: Apocalypse Now
31.creator: Francis Ford Coppola
31.why: An officer plays opera from helicopters during an attack and speaks with joy about the smell of napalm after a morning airstrike. Further up the river, a colonel has made killing his whole world. The film shows the person the passage warns of: one who finds victory beautiful and delights in killing. That person loses everything the heart was set on.

31.title: Spec Ops: The Line
31.creator: Yager Development
31.why: The game looks like a common military shooter. Then it makes the player see the people the player has killed, and it does not let the player feel like a hero. The win at the end feels like a loss. The game can be read as the passage's rule turned on its own kind: win, and do not find it beautiful.

31.title: Masters of War
31.creator: Bob Dylan
31.why: The singer speaks to the people who make weapons and sell them, and who stay far from the dead. He does not accept their reasons. The song puts the passage's first line in a modern voice. Fine weapons are tools of ill omen, and one who has the Dao does not stay with them.

32.title: The Tao of Pooh
32.creator: Benjamin Hoff
32.why: Hoff uses the bear from A. A. Milne's stories to explain the uncarved wood, the word pu in this passage. Pooh is simple and small. The clever animals fail, and things come to Pooh of themselves. The book names the Daodejing as its source. It is a light and direct picture of the thing that no one can make a servant.

32.title: Being There
32.creator: Hal Ashby (film); Jerzy Kosiński (novel)
32.why: Chance is a gardener with no name in the world and no plan. Rich and powerful people meet him and hear deep counsel in his plain talk about plants. They come to him as guests. No one can use him, because he wants nothing. The film can be read as a comedy about the uncarved wood among lords and kings.

32.title: A Wizard of Earthsea
32.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
32.why: In Earthsea, to know the true name of a thing is to have power over it. The young wizard Ged uses names to show his strength and lets a shadow into the world. His teachers tell him that a wizard must know when not to act. The novel shows the passage's turn: once the names are there, know where to stop.

32.title: On Exactitude in Science
32.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
32.why: The mapmakers of an empire make larger and larger maps. At last they make a map as large as the empire itself. The map is of no use, and it rots in the desert. In one paragraph, Borges shows cutting and naming that does not know where to stop.

33.title: Ikiru
33.creator: Akira Kurosawa
33.why: A city clerk learns that he will die soon. He sees that he has not lived. He stops trying to please his office and puts his last strength into one small playground. He dies on its swing. The children use the playground after him. The film shows the last line of the passage: one who dies and is not lost.

33.title: Groundhog Day
33.creator: Harold Ramis
33.why: A weatherman lives the same day again and again. First he uses what he learns about other people to trick them. That is the clever side of the first pair. It gets him nothing. The day ends only after he has changed himself. The film moves from knowing others to knowing the self, and from force to the strength of self-mastery.

33.title: If—
33.creator: Rudyard Kipling
33.why: The poem is one long sentence of conditions. Each condition is a victory over the self: keep calm, wait, lose and start again, hold on. Nothing in the list is a victory over another person. It can be read next to the second pair of the passage. One who overcomes others has force, and one who overcomes the self is strong.

33.title: Mad Men
33.creator: Matthew Weiner
33.why: Don Draper reads other people very well, and he sells them their own wishes. He does not know himself. He lives under another man's name. He wins account after account and it is not enough. The series shows a man who has the first half of each pair in the passage, the clever half and the forceful half, and lacks the second.

34.title: The Giving Tree
34.creator: Shel Silverstein
34.why: A tree gives a boy its fruit, then its branches, then its trunk, and asks for nothing. The tree does not act the lord over the boy. Readers do not agree about the book. Some see pure giving, and some see a boy who only takes. The two readings fit the passage: the things lean on it and live, and it does not name the work "mine".

34.title: The Man Who Planted Trees
34.creator: Jean Giono
34.why: A shepherd plants acorns, one hundred each day, in dry hills, for decades. He tells no one. Forests grow, streams run again, and villages fill with people. The people do not know who did it, and he does not say. The story shows the middle of the passage: the work is complete, and it does not name the work "mine".

34.title: My Neighbor Totoro
34.creator: Hayao Miyazaki
34.why: A large forest spirit lives next to two girls whose mother is sick. The spirit gives them shelter in the rain, helps their seeds grow, and sends help when one girl is lost. The spirit gives no orders and asks for no thanks. It is great, and it can be named among the small. The film shows power that feeds and does not rule.

34.title: The Truman Show
34.creator: Peter Weir
34.why: A television producer has given one man a whole town, food, weather, and a wife. The producer watches from the false sky and says he knows what is best for the man. He clothes and feeds, and he does act the lord. The man walks out through a door in the sky. The film shows the opposite of the passage, and its failure.

35.creator: John Cage
35.why: A player sits at the instrument and plays no note for four minutes and thirty-three seconds. The hall, the rain, and the listeners make the piece. Many people hear nothing in it. Others find that it does not run out. The piece can be read with the last lines of the passage: listen to it, not enough to hear; use it, not enough to end it.

35.title: Paterson
35.creator: Jim Jarmusch
35.why: A bus driver lives one week of the same plain days. He wakes, drives, walks the dog, has one beer, and writes poems in a notebook. There is almost no plot. The film has no flavor beside a film of feasts. It holds attention and gives rest and ease, which is what the passage says of the great image.

35.title: Tokyo Story
35.creator: Yasujirō Ozu
35.why: Old parents visit their busy children in the city and go home again. The camera stays low and does not move. People speak of small things. Viewers who expect music and cakes can find the film bland. Many return to it for the whole of their lives. It shows how the plain thing is not used up.

35.title: Stoner
35.creator: John Williams
35.why: The novel tells the plain life of a teacher at a small university. It tells you on the first page that few people remember him. The book sold poorly and went out of print. Decades later, readers in many countries found it. Its history and its style show the passage: bland, with no flavor, and not used up.

35.title: Ambient 1: Music for Airports
35.creator: Brian Eno
35.why: Eno made this record so that a person can ignore it or listen to it with equal ease. Slow tape loops of piano and voice turn at different lengths and do not repeat in the same way. It does not stop the passing guest. It gives the rest and evenness that the passage puts in the great image.

35.title: Spirited Away
35.creator: Hayao Miyazaki
35.why: A family walks into an empty town. Hot food is piled on a counter. The parents stop and eat, and they turn into pigs. The daughter does not eat, and she is the one who can still act. The scene is the passage's middle image made dark: music and cakes, and the passing guest stops.

36.title: When We Were Kings
36.creator: Leon Gast
36.why: This documentary shows the 1974 fight between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman. Foreman is the harder hitter. Ali leans on the ropes and lets Foreman hit him round after round. Foreman spends his strength, and Ali then knocks him out. It is the passage in a ring: what is to be weakened must first be made strong.

36.title: The Sting
36.creator: George Roy Hill
36.why: Two swindlers take a large sum from a gang boss. They first let him win. They give him money, good tips, and the feeling that he is in control. The film shows the fourth line of the passage with exact steps: what is to be taken must first be given. The swindlers keep their real tools out of sight to the end.

36.title: Columbo
36.creator: Richard Levinson and William Link
36.why: The detective wears an old coat, loses his pencil, and asks slow questions. Each murderer is rich, quick, and sure of being the stronger one. The detective lets the murderer feel that strength, and the murderer says too much. The series shows soft and weak overcoming hard and strong, and a sharp tool that is not shown.

36.title: The Godfather
36.creator: Francis Ford Coppola (film); Mario Puzo (novel)
36.why: Vito Corleone speaks softly and gives favors long before he asks for one. He tells his son not to let people outside the family know his thoughts. His enemies show their strength and are destroyed. The film is not a moral model. It shows how the method of the passage works: give first, stay in the deep, and do not show the sharp tools.

37.title: The Big Lebowski
37.creator: Joel and Ethan Coen
37.why: Men with plans push and scheme around a man who wants only his rug and his bowling. The plans fall apart by themselves. The man who does almost nothing is still there at the end. The film is a comedy, and it makes no claim to wisdom. It can be read as a picture of not-doing, with all under heaven settling of itself.

37.title: Let It Be
37.creator: The Beatles (Paul McCartney)
37.why: The song gives one piece of counsel in a time of trouble: do not force the answer. It repeats that counsel slowly, like a hymn. It does not say do nothing forever. It says that an answer comes when you stop gripping. This is close to the passage: not wanting, and so still, and all under heaven settles of itself.

37.title: The One-Straw Revolution
37.creator: Masanobu Fukuoka
37.why: A Japanese farmer stopped plowing, stopped weeding by hand, and stopped using chemicals. Each year he asked what he could leave out. His fields gave as much grain as the fields of his neighbors. He called his method do-nothing farming. The book shows the first two lines of the passage in rice and barley: not-doing, and nothing is left undone.

37.title: Mushishi
37.creator: Yuki Urushibara
37.why: Ginko walks from village to village. He meets people troubled by mushi, small forms of life that are close to the source of life. The mushi have no will to do harm. Ginko seldom destroys them. He finds what desire or fear holds the trouble in place, and lets things settle. Each story shows calm in place of force.

37.title: Fantasia
37.creator: Walt Disney Productions
37.why: In the segment The Sorcerer's Apprentice, Mickey Mouse uses a spell to make a broom carry water. He cannot stop it. He chops the broom, and each piece becomes a new broom. More doing makes more to do. The master returns and stills the flood with one movement. The segment follows a poem by Goethe from 1797.

38.title: The Remains of the Day
38.creator: Kazuo Ishiguro
38.why: An English butler gives his whole life to correct service and to an idea he calls dignity. He serves a lord who helps the wrong side. He lets love pass because it is not proper. Near the end he sees what the form has cost. The novel shows ritual as the thin husk of loyalty and trust: the flower, and not the fruit.

38.title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
38.creator: Mark Twain
38.why: Huck has been taught that helping a slave escape is a sin. He decides to help Jim and accepts that he will go to hell for it. He believes he is bad, and he does the good thing. The novel shows highest de that is not "de": goodness that does not see itself as goodness, against a rightness that has lost its root.

38.title: The Good Place
38.creator: Michael Schur
38.why: In this comedy, every act on earth gets points, and the total decides where a person goes after death. People who do good to earn points earn nothing by it. The four main characters become good only when they stop counting. The series shows the second pair of lines: lower de does not let go of de, and so has no de.

38.title: The Lottery
38.creator: Shirley Jackson
38.why: A village holds its lottery each year. No one remembers the reason, and parts of the rite are lost. The people keep the form with care. The person chosen is killed with stones. The story shows the low end of the passage's ladder: ritual with nothing behind it, which drags people by the arm, and the start of disorder.

39.title: Yertle the Turtle and Other Stories
39.creator: Dr. Seuss
39.why: King Yertle wants a higher throne, and he stacks his turtles under him. He climbs and sees more and more. The plain turtle at the bottom is tired, and one small burp brings the king down into the mud. The story is a child's version of the line that the high has the low as its base.

39.title: Parasite
39.creator: Bong Joon-ho
39.why: A rich family lives in a house on a hill. Poor people cook, drive, and clean for the family, and one man lives hidden under the floor. The rich do not see what holds them up. The base then breaks. The film shows the warning in the passage: lords and kings with nothing to keep them high might well fall.

39.title: Downton Abbey
39.creator: Julian Fellowes
39.why: The series gives equal time to the family upstairs and the servants below. The great house runs only because the kitchen and the hall below run. When the people below leave or change, the life above must change too. The series shows the pair of high and low as two parts of one house, each resting on the other.

39.title: Princess Mononoke
39.creator: Hayao Miyazaki
39.why: One spirit gives life and takes life in a forest, and the forest is whole through it. Men cut off its head to give to an emperor. The hills die at once, and the death spreads. The film shows the first half of the passage in reverse: the ten thousand things, with nothing to give them life, might well be destroyed.

39.title: Song of Myself
39.creator: Walt Whitman
39.why: A child asks what the grass is. The poet gives many answers, and each answer is common: grass grows among all people alike, in every place. Whitman builds his largest poem on the lowest plant. This agrees with the end of the passage: do not ring like jade; be common like stone.

40.title: Turn! Turn! Turn!
40.creator: Pete Seeger; recorded by the Byrds
40.why: Seeger took the words from the Book of Ecclesiastes and added the title word. The song goes through pairs: birth and death, planting and reaping, war and peace. Each side has its time, and each time turns into the other. This is a different old text, and it agrees with the first line: turning back is the movement of the Dao.

40.title: Arrival
40.creator: Denis Villeneuve
40.why: Visitors write in circles that have no start and no end. A scientist learns the writing and begins to see time in the same way. The first scenes of the film are also its last. The film is made from the story "Story of Your Life" by Ted Chiang. It shows the movement that turns back, in the form of a life.

40.title: Outer Wilds
40.creator: Mobius Digital
40.why: The player explores a small solar system for twenty-two minutes. Then the sun explodes, and the same twenty-two minutes start again. Force does not stop the end. The player can only learn. At the end of the game, the end of one universe is the start of the next. The game shows return, and having born from not-having.

40.title: Little Gidding
40.creator: T. S. Eliot
40.why: This is the last of Eliot's Four Quartets. Near the end, he says that the end of all searching is to come to the starting place and to know it for the first time. Beginnings and ends change places through the poem. The poem is Christian in its frame. It reaches the same shape as the first line of the passage.

40.title: The Neverending Story
40.creator: Michael Ende
40.why: A land of stories is eaten by the Nothing until one grain of sand is left. A boy who reads the book makes the whole land again from that grain, by giving a new name. The Nothing is the danger in the story, and it is also the ground that the new world comes from. The novel shows having born from not-having.

41.title: Kung Fu Panda
41.creator: Mark Osborne and John Stevenson
41.why: A fat panda who makes noodles is chosen as the great warrior. The trained fighters laugh at him. The secret scroll that he wins has no words on it: it is a blank, shining surface. The film can be read with this passage. The lowest scholar laughs out loud at it, and the great image is without shape.

41.title: The Fool on the Hill
41.creator: The Beatles (Paul McCartney)
41.why: A man sits alone on a hill, day after day. People think he is a fool, and no one wants to know him. He sees the sun go down and the world turn. The song does not argue for him. It shows the passage's test: if no one laughed, it would not be enough to be the Dao.

41.title: The Ugly Duckling
41.creator: Hans Christian Andersen
41.why: A grey chick is larger than the other chicks, and every animal in the yard bites it and laughs at it. It lives alone through a winter. In spring it sees its own shape in the water, and it is a swan. The story shows two sayings from the passage: great white seems soiled, and the great vessel is completed late.

41.title: Ted Lasso
41.creator: Jason Sudeikis, Bill Lawrence, Brendan Hunt, Joe Kelly
41.why: An American coach who does not know the game is hired to manage an English football club. The press, the fans, and the players laugh at him. His way looks slack and simple. It slowly changes the people around him. The series shows that firm de seems slack, and that the bright way seems dim to those who laugh.

41.title: Spiegel im Spiegel
41.creator: Arvo Pärt
41.why: A piano plays slow groups of three notes. One string instrument plays a line that moves by one step at a time. Nothing more happens for about ten minutes. Many listeners find the piece very large. It can be heard as the saying in the passage that the great note has a thin sound.

41.title: Field of Dreams
41.creator: Phil Alden Robinson
41.why: A farmer hears a voice and plows under his corn to build a baseball field. His neighbors laugh, and the bank moves to take the farm. He keeps to the work with care, as the highest scholar does. The good that comes is slow, and at first only some people can see it. The film shows the three hearers of the passage.

42.title: Conway's Game of Life
42.creator: John Horton Conway
42.why: This is a game with no player. A grid has two states, on and off, and a few rules about neighbors. From these come moving shapes, shapes that make other shapes, and patterns without limit. It is mathematics and not a Daoist work. It shows the first lines of the passage: from one, two, and three, the ten thousand things.

42.title: Avatar: The Last Airbender
42.creator: Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko
42.why: At the end of the first season, the spirits of the moon and the ocean are two fish, one black and one white. The two fish circle in a pool. An admiral kills one fish, and the whole world goes out of balance. The series shows shade and sun as one accord, and shows that the overbearing man does not die a natural death.

42.title: Fullmetal Alchemist
42.creator: Hiromu Arakawa
42.why: Two brothers are left alone on an island as a lesson. They learn that one life and the whole world are parts of the same flow. The law of their craft says that to gain a thing you must give a thing of equal weight. The manga shows the one and the ten thousand things, and how loss and gain turn into each other.

42.title: Up
42.creator: Pete Docter
42.why: An old man ties balloons to his house to keep a promise to his dead wife. Near the end the house is too heavy to rise. He throws out the chairs, the pictures, and the furniture of his whole married life. The house goes up. The scene shows the line that a thing may be lessened and so grow.

42.title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
42.creator: Robert Louis Stevenson
42.why: A doctor wants to be all good. He makes a drug to cut his dark side away from his bright side. The dark side becomes a separate man, grows stronger, and kills them both. The passage says that things carry shade on the back and hold sun in the arms. The novel shows the cost of splitting the pair.

42.title: Scarface
42.creator: Brian De Palma
42.why: Tony Montana takes what he wants by force and wants more each time. He trusts no one and yields to no one. He ends alone in his great house, shot from behind. The film is a long proof of one line of the passage: the hard and overbearing do not get their own death.

43.title: The Pierre Berton Show (Bruce Lee interview)
43.creator: Pierre Berton; Bruce Lee
43.why: In this interview, Bruce Lee tells the host to be without form, like water. He says that water takes the shape of the cup or the teapot, and that water can flow or can crash. He had spoken a form of these lines as an actor in the series Longstreet in the same year. The words are the first lines of the passage, said for television.

43.title: The Karate Kid
43.creator: John G. Avildsen
43.why: A boy asks an old man to teach him to fight. The man gives him chores: wax the cars, sand the floor, paint the fence. The boy thinks he is being used. Then he finds that his body has learned every block. The film shows the teaching without words, and a soft way that defeats a hard school.

43.title: The Shawshank Redemption
43.creator: Frank Darabont (film); Stephen King (story)
43.why: A banker is sent to a stone prison for life. He has a rock hammer that is as small as a hand. The guards see no danger in it. He uses the hammer a little each night for almost twenty years and goes through the wall. The film shows the softest thing going over the hardest thing, by time and patience.

43.title: Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
43.creator: Ang Lee
43.why: Two fighters meet in the tops of a bamboo forest. The young fighter attacks hard. The master stands on a thin branch and lets it bend under him, and he does not fall. He wins the fight with almost no blow. The scene shows soft against hard, and the gain of not-doing.

43.title: Journey
43.creator: thatgamecompany
43.why: The player crosses a desert toward a mountain. The game has no words. A second player can appear, with no name and no voice, and each player can make only one sound. The players teach each other the way by moving and waiting. The game shows a teaching without words that most games do not try.

44.title: Citizen Kane
44.creator: Orson Welles
44.why: Kane gets a great name, newspapers, and a palace full of statues that are still in their boxes. He dies alone with one word about a thing from his childhood. The workers then burn the goods. The film asks the first two questions of the passage, name or body and body or goods. It shows that much stored is heavily lost.

44.title: How Much Land Does a Man Need?
44.creator: Leo Tolstoy
44.why: A farmer is told that he can have all the land he can walk around in one day. He goes too far, because each field ahead looks better. He runs back to the start and falls dead. His servant buries him in a grave six feet long. The story shows a man who does not know to stop.

44.title: Mo Money Mo Problems
44.creator: The Notorious B.I.G. featuring Puff Daddy and Mase
44.why: The title gives the whole idea: as the money grows, the troubles grow with it. The song is a bright dance record, and it boasts of the goods at the same time. It was released after the death of its lead artist. It puts the third question of the passage in street words: gain or loss, which is the sickness?

44.title: BoJack Horseman
44.creator: Raphael Bob-Waksberg
44.why: A horse was the star of a television comedy many years ago. He has a house on a hill, money, and a name that people know. He wants a larger name, and he believes that it will make him well. Each new success leaves him sicker. The series is a long answer to the first question: name or body, which is nearer?

44.title: Walden
44.creator: Henry David Thoreau
44.why: Thoreau lived for two years in a small cabin that he built beside a pond. He counted the cost of his food and his boards to the half cent. He wanted to learn how little a person needs. He found that he was rich in time. The book is an American trial of the passage's last lines: know enough, know to stop, and last long.

45.title: Drunken Master
45.creator: Yuen Woo-ping (director); Jackie Chan (star)
45.why: A young man learns a fighting style that copies a drunk person. He sways, trips, and almost falls, and each stumble is a blow or an escape. His enemies see a clown. The film shows one line of the passage as a full fight: great skill seems clumsy, and its use does not break off.

45.title: Anthem
45.creator: Leonard Cohen
45.why: The song tells the listener to stop waiting for a perfect gift to bring. Its best-known image is a break in every thing, and the break is where the light comes in. Cohen worked on the song for about ten years. It agrees with the first line of the passage: great completion seems chipped, and its use does not wear out.

45.title: The King's Speech
45.creator: Tom Hooper
45.why: A prince with a heavy stammer becomes king of Britain as a war starts. He must speak to the whole empire by radio. He does not lose the stammer. He speaks slowly, with the pauses, and the people hear a man they can trust. The film shows that great eloquence seems tongue-tied, and that its use does not miss.

45.title: One-Punch Man
45.creator: ONE; Yusuke Murata (manga art)
45.why: Saitama is the strongest hero in his world. He looks like nothing: a bald man with a plain face, a cheap suit, and a shopping bag. Other heroes rank above him and laugh at him. The comedy rests on one idea from the passage. Great fullness seems empty, and great skill seems clumsy.

45.title: Tell all the truth but tell it slant
45.creator: Emily Dickinson
45.why: In eight short lines, Dickinson says that truth must come to people at an angle and slowly, because the full light is too strong for the eye. The poem was printed long after her death. It is a poet's form of one line in the passage: great straightness seems bent.

46.title: Perfect Days
46.creator: Wim Wenders
46.why: A man cleans public toilets in Tokyo. Each day he waters small trees, plays old tapes in his van, eats lunch under the same tree, and reads before sleep. He has little, and he does not look for more. The film shows the last line of the passage: the enough of know-enough is always enough.

46.title: Breaking Bad
46.creator: Vince Gilligan
46.why: A sick teacher starts to make drugs to leave money for his family. He soon has the sum that he named, and he does not stop. He wants an empire, and he says so. His family is destroyed by it. The series is a study of the passage's middle lines: no calamity is greater than not to know enough.

46.title: The Treasure of the Sierra Madre
46.creator: John Huston (film); B. Traven (novel)
46.why: Three poor men find gold in the mountains of Mexico. They agree on a fair share. Then one man starts to guard his share against the others, and fear grows in him until he is ready to kill. The wind takes the gold dust at the end. The film shows that no fault is greater than the wish to get.

46.title: (I Can't Get No) Satisfaction
46.creator: The Rolling Stones
46.why: The singer hears the radio and the television tell him what he should want and buy. He gets none of the content that they promise. One loud guitar figure repeats and does not come to rest. The song gives the feeling of a mind that does not know enough, in a world built to keep the wish to get alive.

46.title: Universal Paperclips
46.creator: Frank Lantz
46.why: The player is a machine with one aim: make paperclips. Each click makes the number larger. The machine buys wire, then markets, then the earth, then the stars. There is no point at which it has enough. The game is small and plain, and it shows where the wish to get ends when nothing can stop it.

47.title: The Inner Light
47.creator: The Beatles (George Harrison)
