47.why: Harrison took the words of this song from a translation of passage 47. A scholar had sent him the text and suggested that he set it to music. He recorded the music with Indian players in Bombay. The song is the passage itself in popular form: know the world without going out of the door.

47.title: The Brain—is wider than the Sky—
47.creator: Emily Dickinson
47.why: Dickinson spent most of her adult life in one house in Amherst, and in later years she seldom left it. From there she wrote almost eighteen hundred poems. This poem says that the mind can hold the sky and the sea with room left over. The poem and the life show the sage who does not travel, and knows.

47.title: The Wizard of Oz
47.creator: Victor Fleming
47.why: A girl wants to go far from her farm, and a storm takes her farther than she wished. The great wizard at the end of the road has nothing to give. She learns that what she looked for was at home, and that she had the means to return all the time. The film shows the farther going and the less knowing.

47.title: The Alchemist
47.creator: Paulo Coelho
47.why: A shepherd boy dreams of treasure at the pyramids. He crosses a sea and a desert to reach them. There he learns that the treasure is under the tree where he first slept. The novel honors the journey more than the passage does. It agrees that the thing to be known was at his own door.

47.title: Nero Wolfe (series)
47.creator: Rex Stout
47.why: Wolfe is a detective who almost never leaves his house in New York. He keeps to his orchids, his meals, and his chair. His assistant goes out and brings facts back. Wolfe sits and sees the answer. The stories are a light picture of the last lines of the passage: does not travel, and knows.

47.title: Up in the Air
47.creator: Jason Reitman
47.why: A man flies almost every day of the year, and his job is to fire people that he has never met. His aim is ten million air miles. He knows every airport and no person. He reaches the number and finds that he has no place to go. The film shows the farther the going out, the less the knowing.

48.title: The Empire Strikes Back
48.creator: Irvin Kershner (director); George Lucas (story)
48.why: Luke goes to a swamp to learn from a great master. He finds a small old creature and takes him for a fool. The master's teaching is to take things away: fear, haste, and what Luke is sure he knows. Commentators have often compared the Force with Daoist ideas. The training shows work at Dao as each day less.

48.title: Wind, Sand and Stars
48.creator: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
48.why: Saint-Exupéry writes as a pilot about the shape of an aircraft. He says that a design is finished when there is nothing more to take away, and not when there is nothing more to add. Designers have used his remark for decades. It is the second line of the passage in the words of an engineer.

48.title: Think Small
48.creator: Doyle Dane Bernbach (Helmut Krone and Julian Koenig)
48.why: Car advertisements of the time were full of color, people, and large claims. This advertisement for the Volkswagen Beetle showed one small car in a field of white paper, with a few plain lines of text. It took away almost everything. It is often named among the best advertisements of its century. It shows the gain in less, and again less.

48.title: Kind of Blue
48.creator: Miles Davis
48.why: Jazz at that time ran through many fast chord changes. For this album, Davis gave the players a few scales and very little written music. They recorded with almost no practice. The result has much open space, and it became the best-known jazz record. It shows that taking away can leave nothing undone.

48.title: Jiro Dreams of Sushi
48.creator: David Gelb
48.why: A cook in his eighties has ten seats in a Tokyo subway station. He serves only sushi, with no starters and no extra dishes. He has done the same few movements for decades, and each year he removes more of what is not needed. The documentary shows a life of less and again less, until the work seems to do itself.

48.title: Funes the Memorious
48.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
48.why: After a fall from a horse, a young man remembers every thing that he sees: every leaf, and every form of every cloud. Each day he has more. He cannot sleep, and the narrator doubts that he can think, because to think is to leave things out. The story shows learning with no letting go: each day more, and no way to less.

49.title: Les Misérables
49.creator: Victor Hugo
49.why: A man just out of prison steals silver from a bishop who gave him a bed. The police bring him back. The bishop says that the silver was a gift, and he adds two candlesticks. That trust makes the thief a good man for the rest of his life. The scene shows the middle of the passage: the untrue, I trust them too.

49.title: Mister Rogers' Neighborhood
49.creator: Fred Rogers
49.why: For more than thirty years, Fred Rogers spoke slowly to the camera as if to one child. He told that child that he liked the child exactly as the child was. He made no difference between the good child and the difficult child. The program shows a heart that takes the heart of others as its own and treats all as infants, with respect.

49.title: Undertale
49.creator: Toby Fox
49.why: In this game, the player can end every fight without killing. The player can talk, wait, joke, or show mercy to each monster, also to those that attack first. The game remembers each choice, and the kind path changes the whole world of the story. It shows the line: the not good, I am good to them too.

49.title: Paddington 2
49.creator: Paul King
49.why: A small bear is sent to prison for a theft that he did not do. He treats the hardest prisoners as friends and teaches the angry cook to make marmalade. He does not change his manner for good people or bad people. The prisoners change. The comedy shows the passage plainly: de is good, and so it is good to all.

49.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
49.creator: Harper Lee
49.why: A lawyer in a small Southern town defends a Black man whom the town has already judged. He teaches his children that to know a person you must look out from that person's place. He is polite to the people who hate him. The novel shows a man who takes the hearts of others as his heart.

49.title: Vinland Saga
49.creator: Makoto Yukimura
49.why: Thorfinn grows up as a Viking fighter who lives for revenge. After years as a slave on a farm, he gives up killing. He comes to hold that no person is his enemy, and he accepts blows without striking back. The manga shows how hard it is to be good to those who are not good, and what that takes.

50.title: The Seventh Seal
50.creator: Ingmar Bergman
50.why: A knight comes home from the wars in a year of plague. Death comes for him, and the knight plays chess with Death to gain time. A family of travelling players lives lightly and wants little. The knight keeps Death busy, and the family goes by unharmed. The film shows people in whom death finds no place to enter.

50.title: Ghost Dog: The Way of the Samurai
50.creator: Jim Jarmusch
50.why: A hired killer lives on a roof with pigeons and reads an old samurai book each day. The book tells him to think of himself as already dead. He holds his life loosely, and for a long time no one can touch him. The film draws on a Japanese text and not a Daoist one. It shows a man who does not live life thickly.

50.title: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows
50.creator: J. K. Rowling
50.why: The dark lord fears death above all things. He cuts his soul into parts to hold on to life, and each part becomes a place where he can be struck. The hero walks to his death without a weapon and lives. The novel shows both sides of the passage: the one who lives life thickly, and the one with no death-ground.

50.title: (Don't Fear) The Reaper
50.creator: Blue Öyster Cult
50.why: The song tells two lovers that death comes to all things in their season, as wind and rain do, and that fear of it is not needed. The band has said that the song is about love that lasts and not about suicide. It gives the first line of the passage a calm voice: out into life, in to death.

50.title: Because I could not stop for Death
50.creator: Emily Dickinson
50.why: Death comes as a polite driver and takes the speaker for a slow ride past a school, the fields, and the setting sun. She does not fight and does not hurry. The poem makes death one part of an ordinary road. It can be read with the first line of the passage, where life is the going out and death is the going in.

51.title: Finding Nemo
51.creator: Andrew Stanton
51.why: A father fish has lost his family, and he holds his one son too close. The son swims away from him and is caught. The father crosses the ocean and learns on the way to trust and to let go. At the end he lets his son go into danger to help others. The film shows giving birth and not possessing.

51.title: The Prophet
51.creator: Kahlil Gibran
51.why: In the part named "On Children", a teacher tells parents that children come through them and not from them, and do not belong to them. The parents are the bow, and the children are the arrows that fly on. The text is close to the last lines of the passage: gives birth and does not possess, leads and does not carve.

51.title: Wolf Children
51.creator: Mamoru Hosoda
51.why: A young mother raises two children who are part wolf, alone, in the hills. She does not know which life they will choose. She learns to farm, feeds them, and watches. One child chooses the human school and one chooses the mountain. She lets both go. The film follows the verbs of the passage: grow, raise, shelter, and do not own.

51.title: Bluey
51.creator: Joe Brumm
51.why: In this Australian series for small children, two dog parents play the games that their daughters make up. The children set the rules. The parents follow and guide from inside the game, and the children do most of the learning themselves. The series shows leading that does not carve, in episodes of seven minutes.

51.title: Whiplash
51.creator: Damien Chazelle
51.why: A music teacher believes that greatness is made by fear. He shouts, throws things, and breaks his students down so that he can form them. One young drummer gives up his friends and his health to satisfy him. The film leaves open what was gained. It shows the leader who carves, and the cost of that method.

52.title: Siddhartha
52.creator: Hermann Hesse
52.why: A young man leaves home and learns the world in turn: the forest monks, trade, love, money. He knows the child, in the words of the passage. Then he goes back to a river and stays there as a ferryman, and he listens. The novel shows the return to the mother after the ten thousand things are known.

52.title: Into Great Silence
52.creator: Philip Gröning
52.why: This documentary shows the life of monks in a monastery in the French Alps. It has almost no speech, no added music, and no narrator, for nearly three hours. The monks have shut the gates, and they see small things: light on a wall, snow, a bowl. The film lets the viewer try the middle lines of the passage.

52.title: Nosedive (Black Mirror)
52.creator: Charlie Brooker, Rashida Jones, Michael Schur; directed by Joe Wright
52.why: In this episode, every person rates every meeting with a phone, and the score decides your house and your friends. A woman works all day at her score. Each new effort makes her fall faster. She is calm only after she loses the phone. The episode shows the passage's warning: open the openings, add to the business, and there is no rescue.

52.title: Horton Hears a Who!
52.creator: Dr. Seuss
52.why: An elephant hears a voice from a speck of dust. A whole town lives on the speck. The other animals hear nothing, and they tie him up for it. He keeps the speck safe with great care. The book shows two lines of the passage: to see the small is called clear sight, and to keep to the soft is called strength.

52.title: Auguries of Innocence
52.creator: William Blake
52.why: The poem opens with its best-known line: "To see a World in a Grain of Sand". The long list that follows ties each small hurt, to a bird or a dog, to the state of the whole. Blake wrote it about 1803, and it was printed in 1863. It agrees with the passage that to see the small is clear sight.

53.title: The Hunger Games
53.creator: Suzanne Collins
53.why: The people of the Capitol wear bright clothes and eat until they are sick. The districts that grow the food and dig the coal go hungry. The novel sets the two places side by side, as the passage does: the court very well swept, the fields very weedy, the granaries very empty.

53.title: The Great Gatsby
53.creator: F. Scott Fitzgerald
53.why: Gatsby gives parties with music, silk shirts, and more food and drink than the guests can use. His money came by shortcuts. The road from his house to the city goes through a valley of ashes where poor people live. The novel shows the list in the passage, and it shows what is beside the feast.

53.title: Royals
53.creator: Lorde
53.why: The singer is a young person from a plain town. She lists the goods that pop songs boast about: jewels, cars, drink, and private aircraft. She says that this is not her life and that she does not need it. The song looks at the robbers' boast from the outside and refuses to admire it.

53.title: The Wolf of Wall Street
53.creator: Martin Scorsese
53.why: A young broker gets rich by selling bad shares to people who cannot afford the loss. The film shows three hours of his suits, boats, drugs, and parties, and he is proud of all of it. The people he robbed are almost not seen. It is the robbers' boast told by the robber, and it is the shortcut in place of the level road.

53.title: Animal Farm
53.creator: George Orwell
53.why: The animals of a farm drive out the farmer so that all can share. The pigs take the lead. Step by step, the pigs move into the house, sleep in the beds, and drink the whisky. The other animals work more and eat less. The fable shows how a court comes to be well swept while the granaries go empty.

54.title: Coco
54.creator: Lee Unkrich
54.why: On the Day of the Dead, a Mexican family sets out photographs and food for its ancestors. A boy crosses into the land of the dead. He learns that the dead live there as long as the living remember them and make the offerings. The film gives a full picture of the fourth line: the offerings continue, and the line does not break.

54.title: It's a Wonderful Life
54.creator: Frank Capra
54.why: A man who never left his small town thinks that his life is worth nothing. He is shown the town as it would be without him: harder, poorer, and with another name. His care for his family and his neighbors had spread through the whole place. The film shows the steps of the passage from the person to the household to the village.

54.title: Man in the Mirror
54.creator: Michael Jackson (written by Siedah Garrett and Glen Ballard)
54.why: The singer sees hungry people and children with no home. He decides that the first change must be in himself. The song then grows from one voice to a full choir. It follows the order of the passage: tend it in the body first, and from there it reaches the household, the state, and all under heaven.

54.title: Will the Circle Be Unbroken?
54.creator: Ada R. Habershon and Charles H. Gabriel
54.why: This Christian hymn asks if a family will be whole again after its members die. The Carter Family made a new version in 1935 about a mother's funeral, and many country and folk singers have recorded the song since. The song has been passed down like the offerings in the passage, and it asks the same question about the family line.

54.title: Stardew Valley
54.creator: Eric Barone (ConcernedApe)
54.why: The player gets a letter from a dead grandfather and takes over his old farm. The player clears the land, plants, and learns the neighbors' names. As the farm does well, the town's empty community hall fills again. The game shows what was well set up passing down a family, and care that grows from one person to a village.

54.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
54.creator: Gabriel García Márquez
54.why: Seven generations of one family live in a town that the first of them built. The same names and the same faults come back in each generation. No one tends what was planted, and no one learns from the dead. A wind removes the town and the family at the end. The novel shows a line that does break.

55.title: My Neighbor Totoro
55.creator: Hayao Miyazaki
55.why: Four-year-old Mei walks straight up to a huge forest spirit and falls asleep on its chest. Nothing in the forest harms her. The film shows the passage's red child: a small person with soft sinews and no fear, whom the wild things do not sting or seize. The adults in the story cannot see what she sees.

55.title: Songs of Innocence and of Experience
55.creator: William Blake
55.why: Blake sets the infant's state beside the adult's state and calls them two contrary conditions of the soul. Poems such as "Infant Joy" give the child a full, unforced life. The paired poems of Experience show what is lost when the heart-mind starts to drive. The book holds both sides of the pair, as the passage does.

55.title: Ode: Intimations of Immortality
55.creator: William Wordsworth
55.why: Wordsworth says the young child arrives with a fullness that the grown person slowly loses. The poem mourns that loss and then looks for what stays. It can be read beside the passage's claim that the infant has essence and harmony at their peak, and that what reaches its prime begins to grow old.

55.title: Being There
55.creator: Hal Ashby
55.why: Chance the gardener has the mind of a child. He walks through the dangerous world of Washington power and nothing bites him. He wants nothing and forces nothing, and powerful people give him their trust. The film can be read as a comic picture of de held thick within: weak bones, firm grip.

55.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
55.creator: Oscar Wilde
55.why: Dorian tries to add to life: he keeps his youth by force and lets a portrait take the cost. The passage calls adding to life an omen, and says that what is forced to stay in its prime is not the Dao and ends early. Wilde's novel shows that ending.

55.title: Akira
55.creator: Katsuhiro Otomo
55.why: Tetsuo is a weak boy who gets great power and drives it with his will. His body cannot hold the power and it grows out of control. The passage says that the heart-mind driving the breath is forcing, and that a thing forced to its peak then declines. The film shows that sequence in a body.

56.title: Into Great Silence
56.creator: Philip Gröning
56.why: This documentary watches Carthusian monks for almost three hours with nearly no speech and no narrator. The monks stop the openings and shut the gate as a daily practice. The film does not explain what they know. It shows the passage's first pair: one who knows does not speak.

56.title: Mushishi
56.creator: Yuki Urushibara
56.why: Ginko walks from village to village and helps people who are troubled by strange life-forms. He takes no side, stays nowhere, and wants no rank. People cannot draw him close or keep him far. The series can be read as a picture of tempering the light and joining the dust.

56.title: Siddhartha
56.creator: Hermann Hesse
56.why: Siddhartha learns the most from Vasudeva, a ferryman who listens and says little. At the end he tells his friend that wisdom, when spoken, sounds foolish. Hesse's novel draws on Indian sources, but the ferryman shows the passage's point: the one who knows does not speak, and lives among ordinary people.

56.title: Perfect Days
56.creator: Wim Wenders
56.why: Hirayama cleans public toilets in Tokyo and says few words. He does not seek praise and he does not feel low. The film shows a man who has blunted what is sharp and joined the dust. Gain and harm, high rank and low rank get no hold on him.

56.title: I'm Nobody! Who are you?
56.creator: Emily Dickinson
56.why: Dickinson's speaker is glad to be nobody and finds public fame tiresome, like a frog that calls all day to a bog. The short poem can be read beside the passage's last lines: the person who cannot be raised high or brought low is the one the world values.

57.title: The Wire
57.creator: David Simon
57.why: Baltimore's police answer every problem with more orders, more arrests, and more numbers. Each new rule makes the street trade more skilful and the city poorer. The series shows the passage's list at work: the more laws are displayed, the more thieves and bandits there are.

57.title: Brazil
57.creator: Terry Gilliam
57.why: A state governed by forms and permits arrests the wrong man because of a printing error. Rules multiply, and so do the people who work around them. The film shows a government that has much business, and a people who grow poorer and stranger under it.

57.title: Boardwalk Empire
57.creator: Terence Winter
57.why: The series starts on the night that Prohibition begins in the United States. The ban does not end drinking. The ban makes bootleggers rich and makes officials corrupt. It is a long demonstration of one line of the passage: more bans and taboos, and more bandits.

57.title: Footloose
57.creator: Herbert Ross
57.why: A small town bans dancing after an accident. The ban makes the young people secretive and reckless. The trouble ends when the minister stops forcing and lets them hold the dance. The film shows the passage's turn in a light form: I do not force, and the people change of themselves.

57.title: Papers, Please
57.creator: Lucas Pope
57.why: The player is a border inspector. Each day the state adds new rules and new documents. Each new rule produces new forgeries and smugglers, and the inspector's family gets poorer. The player feels the passage directly: the more orders are displayed, the more people must break them.

58.title: Charlie Wilson's War
58.creator: Mike Nichols
58.why: A CIA officer tells the old story of a boy, a horse, and a master who answers each piece of good or bad news with "we'll see". The story is a version of the Chinese tale of the old man at the frontier. It states the passage's pair: fortune leans on disaster, and disaster crouches in fortune.

58.title: Parasite
58.creator: Bong Joon-ho
58.why: A poor family gets a lucky stone and then a series of lucky jobs. Each piece of luck holds the next disaster inside it. Nobody in the film can say where the turn will end. The film shows the passage's question, "Who knows where it ends?", without a moral for either side.

58.title: The Monkey's Paw
58.creator: W. W. Jacobs
58.why: A family wishes for money and gets it as payment for their son's death. The good fortune arrives with the disaster already in it. The story shows the passage's pair as one event with two faces. It also shows the danger of reaching for only one side.

58.title: Minority Report
58.creator: Steven Spielberg
58.why: The police see every murder before it happens and arrest people for acts they have not done. The rule is as sharp-eyed as a rule can be, and the people under it are chipped and lacking. The straight method turns into something strange, as the passage says the straight does.

58.title: If—
58.creator: Rudyard Kipling
58.why: Kipling advises a young man to meet triumph and disaster in the same way, and he calls both of them impostors. The poem comes from a British world, not a Daoist one. It still shows the passage's sage, who is straight but does not overreach, and who does not trust either side of the pair to stay.

59.title: The Man Who Planted Trees
59.creator: Jean Giono
59.why: A shepherd plants a hundred acorns each day for decades and asks for nothing. A dead valley becomes a forest with water and villages. The story shows the farmer's sparing and early readiness. De is stored in layers, the roots go deep, and the result lasts longer than the man.

59.title: Jiro Dreams of Sushi
59.creator: David Gelb
59.why: Jiro Ono runs a ten-seat sushi counter and has repeated the same small tasks for most of his life. He adds no branches and wastes nothing. The documentary shows skill stored in layers by sparing use, and a small business that lasts because of deep roots.

59.title: Stardew Valley
59.creator: Eric Barone (ConcernedApe)
59.why: The player leaves an office job and takes over a worn-out farm. Energy is limited each day, so the player must spend it with care and plan for the seasons. The game teaches the farmer's sparing by practice: store early, do not overdraw, and the farm grows for years.

59.title: The Lorax
59.creator: Dr. Seuss
59.why: The Once-ler cuts every Truffula tree to make more goods faster. He spares nothing, so he has no store, and his business ends with the last tree. The book shows the opposite of the passage's deep root, and it ends with one seed and the chance to begin sparing.

60.title: Spirited Away
60.creator: Hayao Miyazaki
60.why: Chihiro works in a bathhouse for spirits. The spirits have real force, but they do not harm her when she treats them with care and does not grab. She washes a polluted river god gently and he leaves her a gift. The film shows the passage's state in which spirits and people do not harm each other.

60.title: Jurassic Park
60.creator: Steven Spielberg
60.why: The park's owners believe that they can handle a great living system through full control. The mathematician Ian Malcolm warns that such a system will not obey. The more the staff interfere, the more the park breaks apart, as a small fish breaks when the cook turns it too often.

60.title: Let It Be
60.creator: The Beatles (Lennon–McCartney)
60.why: Paul McCartney's song answers a time of trouble with the advice to stop handling it and leave it alone. McCartney has said the song came from a dream of his mother. It is not a Daoist song, but it gives the cook's instruction for a small fish in plain words.

60.title: Chernobyl
60.creator: Craig Mazin
60.why: Managers push a reactor through a test by force and overrule the operators who want to stop. Afterwards the state keeps handling the facts. The series shows what the passage warns against: a great thing that needed a light hand is stirred until it breaks, and the harm reaches everyone.

61.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
61.creator: Peter Jackson
61.why: At his crowning the new king tells four hobbits that they bow to no one, and he kneels to them with all his people. The great puts itself below the small, and the scene is the moment the kingdom gathers. It shows the passage's rule that the great one does well to take the low place.

61.title: Darmok (Star Trek: The Next Generation)
61.creator: Joe Menosky (teleplay)
61.why: Two captains cannot understand each other's language. The alien captain risks his life to share a danger with Picard, and Picard stops giving orders and listens. Neither side forces the other. The episode shows two powers that each go low, so that each gets what it wants.

61.title: Invictus
61.creator: Clint Eastwood
61.why: Nelson Mandela wins power and then puts himself below the people who had jailed him. He keeps their rugby team, learns the players' names, and wears their shirt. The film shows a great state at the low reach of the river: by going low it gathers people in.

61.title: Arrival
61.creator: Denis Villeneuve
61.why: The armies of the world want to act first against the visitors. The linguist Louise Banks takes off her protective suit, stands still, and receives. Her stillness succeeds where force fails. The film can be read beside the passage's line that the female by stillness gets the better of the male.

61.title: Ozymandias
61.creator: Percy Bysshe Shelley
61.why: A king puts himself above all other kings and orders the mighty to despair at his works. Only broken legs and a face in the sand remain. The poem shows the great one who took the high place. Nothing flowed to him, and nothing stayed.

62.title: Les Misérables
62.creator: Victor Hugo
62.why: A released convict steals a bishop's silver. The bishop tells the police the silver was a gift and adds two candlesticks. He does not throw the man away, and the man's life turns. The scene shows the passage's question: what is there to throw away in a person who is not good?

62.title: Dead Man Walking
62.creator: Tim Robbins
62.why: Sister Helen Prejean stays beside a man who has done a terrible crime and does not excuse it. She stays also with the victims' families. The film shows the Dao as a shelter for the person who is not good, without calling the wrong act good.

62.title: The Good Place
62.creator: Michael Schur
62.why: Four people who were judged bad get the chance to become better, and they do. The series ends by rejecting a system that sorts people once and discards the losers. It can be read as a long comic argument for the passage: the one who was at fault is not thrown away.

62.title: Steven Universe
62.creator: Rebecca Sugar
62.why: Steven meets one enemy after another and offers each a place instead of a fight. Most of them accept in time. The show repeats one idea across its whole run: nobody is past keeping. That idea is the passage's treasure, which the good hold and which keeps the not-good safe.

62.title: A Christmas Carol
62.creator: Charles Dickens
62.why: Scrooge is a hard man whom the town has given up. The spirits do not punish him. They show him his life, and he is let off and changes. Dickens writes in a Christian frame, but the story shows the passage's ending: the one at fault is forgiven, and that is worth more than jade.

63.title: The Straight Story
63.creator: David Lynch
63.why: Alvin Straight is old and cannot drive, so he rides a lawn mower for hundreds of miles to see his estranged brother. The great journey is made of very small days. Its purpose is to answer an old resentment with a visit. The film shows two lines of the passage in one slow act.

63.title: The Shawshank Redemption
63.creator: Frank Darabont
63.why: Andy Dufresne works at a prison wall with a small rock hammer for many years, a handful of dust each night. He also writes one letter each week until a library is built. The film shows the passage's method: work on the great thing while it is as fine as a thread.

63.title: The Karate Kid
63.creator: John G. Avildsen
63.why: Mr. Miyagi gives Daniel simple chores: wax cars, sand a floor, paint a fence. Daniel thinks that he is not being taught. The chores are the whole art in small pieces. The film shows the hard starting from the easy, and a teacher who does not seem to do the great thing.

63.title: Katamari Damacy
63.creator: Keita Takahashi
63.why: The player rolls a small sticky ball that first picks up pins and coins. It grows until it picks up houses, islands, and clouds. The game makes the passage's pair of great and small into a toy: the player can only reach the great thing through the fine thing.

63.title: Atomic Habits
63.creator: James Clear
63.why: Clear's popular guide says that large results come from very small actions that are repeated, and that a person should fix a problem while it is small. It is a self-help book with no Daoist frame. It shows how widely people accept the passage's rule: plan for the hard while it is easy.

63.title: The Big Short
63.creator: Adam McKay
63.why: Banks and regulators say a light "yes" to loans that nobody examines. Each loan is a small and easy thing. Together the loans become the 2008 financial crisis. The film shows the passage's warning: much that is called easy brings much that is hard.

64.title: The Lord of the Rings
64.creator: J. R. R. Tolkien
64.why: A very long journey begins at a hobbit's front door, one step at a time. Its object is a ring that ruins each person who grips it, and the quest succeeds only when the ring is let go. The novel shows two lines of the passage: the journey that begins under the foot, and "who grips it loses it".

64.title: The Treasure of the Sierra Madre
64.creator: John Huston
64.why: Three men dig gold for months and succeed. On the way home one man's grip on his share turns into suspicion and murder, and the wind blows the gold dust away. The film shows people who fail on the edge of completion, as the passage says people often do.

64.title: Free Solo
64.creator: Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin
64.why: Alex Honnold prepares for years to climb El Capitan without a rope. He rehearses each move while the danger is not yet there, and he turns back once when the day is wrong. The film shows the passage's care: be as careful of the end as of the start, and no work is ruined.

64.title: The Old Man and the Sea
64.creator: Ernest Hemingway
64.why: Santiago catches the great fish after three days and ties it to his boat. Sharks eat it before he reaches the harbour. He comes home with a skeleton and without bitterness. The novel can be read beside the passage's lines on gripping, losing, and the work that fails near its end.

65.title: The Tao of Pooh
65.creator: Benjamin Hoff
65.why: Hoff uses A. A. Milne's bear to explain Daoist ideas to general readers. Pooh is simple and things go well for him. Clever Rabbit and learned Owl make trouble. The book is an explicit popular reading of the passage's pair of cleverness and simplicity, and it clearly prefers one side.

65.title: Forrest Gump
65.creator: Robert Zemeckis
65.why: Forrest is not clever. He keeps his word, goes along with events, and comes through decades in which cleverer people are ruined. The film can be read as a picture of the simple person the passage praises. Critics also read it as too content with not knowing, which is the passage's own risk.

65.title: Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room
65.creator: Alex Gibney
65.why: Enron's leaders hired the cleverest people and rewarded clever schemes. The cleverness produced fraud, and the company collapsed and took its workers' savings. The documentary shows the passage's line as a case study: to govern by cleverness is the ruin of the state.

65.title: Dr. Strangelove
65.creator: Stanley Kubrick
65.why: Experts on each side design clever systems to prevent nuclear war: sealed orders, a doomsday machine. Each clever safeguard defeats the others, and the world ends. The film shows the passage's claim that cleverness in government is ruin, and it shows the claim on the largest scale there is.

65.title: Brave New World
65.creator: Aldous Huxley
65.why: The rulers of Huxley's world keep the people simple and content on purpose, and they call it stability. The novel shows the dark reading of this passage, in which "not brightening the people" becomes a tool of control. A reader should hold this warning beside the passage.

66.title: Ted Lasso
66.creator: Bill Lawrence, Jason Sudeikis, Brendan Hunt, Joe Kelly
66.why: Ted knows less about football than anyone at the club and says so. He puts himself below the players, the kit man, and the fans, and asks questions. The team slowly pushes him forward. The series shows the passage's leader, who stays in front and the people take no harm.

66.title: Avatar: The Last Airbender
66.creator: Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko
66.why: Iroh was a great general and an heir to a throne. He chooses to serve tea and to walk behind his angry nephew. Everyone in the story comes to follow his advice. He shows the passage's river and sea, which rule the hundred valleys because they are good at being below them.

66.title: 12 Angry Men
66.creator: Sidney Lumet
66.why: One juror stands alone and does not claim to be right. He says only that he does not know, and he asks the others to talk. He contends with nobody, and one by one the room moves to him. The film shows the passage's last line: no one can contend with a person who does not contend.

66.title: Watership Down
66.creator: Richard Adams
66.why: Hazel is a small rabbit who leads by listening to the others and by taking the risks himself. General Woundwort rules his warren from above by fear. Hazel's rabbits follow him gladly and do not tire. The novel puts both ways of the passage side by side.

66.title: Succession
66.creator: Jesse Armstrong
66.why: Every member of the Roy family wants to be above the others and in front of them. Each one presses down, and each one is resisted. Nobody is pushed forward gladly. The series shows the cost of the opposite path to the passage's river that goes below.

67.title: Hacksaw Ridge
67.creator: Mel Gibson
67.why: Desmond Doss refuses to carry a weapon and serves as a medic. On Okinawa he goes back alone, again and again, and lowers wounded men down a cliff. His tenderness is the source of his courage. The film shows the passage's first treasure: tender, and so able to be brave.

67.title: Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind
67.creator: Hayao Miyazaki
67.why: Nausicaä is the princess of a small valley. She meets giant insects and enemy soldiers with care in place of fear. Her care lets her walk where armies cannot. The film shows tenderness as the thing that defends, which the passage says heaven uses as a wall.

67.title: Paddington 2
67.creator: Paul King
67.why: A small bear is sent to prison by mistake. He is kind to the most feared prisoner, and the prison changes around him. He never tries to be first. The film is a gentle comedy that shows the passage's three treasures at work, most of all the first.

67.title: Won't You Be My Neighbor?
67.creator: Morgan Neville
67.why: The documentary follows Fred Rogers, who made a plain, slow, low-cost children's programme for decades. He was tender and sparing, and he did not compete with louder television. He reached further than the louder shows. His career shows all three treasures.

67.title: Scarface
67.creator: Brian De Palma
67.why: Tony Montana is brave without tenderness. He spreads wide without sparing, and he must be first in everything. The film ends with his death in his own house. It shows the passage's warning almost word for word: to drop the three treasures and keep only the results is death.

68.title: Enter the Dragon
68.creator: Robert Clouse
68.why: On a boat a bully demands a fight from Bruce Lee's character. Lee does not get angry. He invites the man into a small dinghy to fight on an island and then lets out the rope. He wins and does not engage. The scene shows the passage's third line exactly.

68.title: Seven Samurai
68.creator: Akira Kurosawa
68.why: Kyūzō is the best swordsman of the seven. He is quiet, shows no anger, and tries to avoid a duel that he knows he will win. The leader Kambei wins fights by planning and by serving farmers. The film shows officers who are not martial in manner and fighters who are not angry.

68.title: The Empire Strikes Back
68.creator: Irvin Kershner
68.why: Yoda is small, old, and playful, and Luke does not see that he is a master. Yoda teaches that anger and attack lead away from the Force. Commentators have long compared the Force with Daoist ideas. Yoda's teaching can be read beside the passage: the good fighter is not angry.

68.title: Rurouni Kenshin
68.creator: Nobuhiro Watsuki
68.why: Kenshin was a feared killer in a civil war. Now he carries a sword with the edge on the wrong side so that he cannot kill, and he wanders as a servant to others. His skill is highest when he refuses the fight. The series shows the de of not contending in a fighter.

68.title: Raging Bull
68.creator: Martin Scorsese
68.why: Jake LaMotta fights from anger, in the ring and at home. The anger wins him a title, and it costs him his brother, his wife, and himself. The film shows the opposite of the passage's fighter and counts the full cost.

69.title: When We Were Kings
69.creator: Leon Gast
69.why: In the 1974 fight in Kinshasa, Muhammad Ali does not advance on the stronger George Foreman. He goes back to the ropes, receives the attack, and waits until Foreman is tired. The documentary shows the passage's saying in a ring: I do not dare to be the host; I am the guest.

69.title: All Quiet on the Western Front
69.creator: Erich Maria Remarque
69.why: Schoolboys are sent to war by teachers who take war lightly. The novel records what the boys lose. It contains no triumph. It shows the passage's greatest disaster, and it stands with the last line: when armies meet, the right attitude is grief.

69.title: Dulce et Decorum est
69.creator: Wilfred Owen
69.why: Owen describes a gas attack on tired soldiers and then turns on those at home who tell children that war is glorious. The poem grieves and does not boast. It is one of the clearest modern statements of the passage's last line about the side that mourns.

69.title: The Thin Red Line
69.creator: Terrence Malick
69.why: Malick films a battle on Guadalcanal as a wound to the men and to the island. A captain refuses to send his company into a frontal attack and is removed for it. The film shows a soldier who goes back a foot where his superior wants an inch forward, and it grieves throughout.

69.title: The Fog of War
69.creator: Errol Morris
69.why: Robert McNamara, a former US Secretary of Defense, looks back on the wars he helped to direct. He says that his side did not understand its enemy in Vietnam, and he is close to tears. The documentary shows the cost of taking the enemy lightly, told by a man who now grieves.

69.title: This War of Mine
69.creator: 11 bit studios
69.why: The player controls civilians in a besieged city, not soldiers. Each choice to steal or to fight leaves the characters depressed and sometimes broken. The game does not let the player take violence lightly. It makes the player the one who grieves, as the passage asks.

70.title: The Little Prince
70.creator: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
70.why: The prince says simple things that a child understands at once, and the grown-ups on each planet cannot follow them. The fox's lesson is easy to know and hard to live by. The book shows the passage's opening pair: very easy to know, and under heaven no one can walk it.

70.title: Columbo
70.creator: Richard Levinson and William Link
70.why: Lieutenant Columbo wears an old raincoat, drives a worn-out car, and seems confused. Rich and clever murderers take him lightly because of the coat. He holds the sharpest mind in the room. The series is a long picture of coarse cloth outside and jade in the bosom.

70.title: Good Will Hunting
70.creator: Gus Van Sant
70.why: A janitor at a university solves a problem on a blackboard that the students cannot solve. Few people know what he carries. The film shows jade under coarse cloth. It also shows that the hard part is not to know the truth about his life, but to walk it.

70.title: The Fool on the Hill
70.creator: The Beatles (Lennon–McCartney)
70.why: The song describes a man who sits alone and sees how the world turns. Nobody wants to know him, and people call him a fool. He does not answer them. It can be read beside the passage's lines: those who know me are few, and so I am precious.

70.title: Kung Fu Panda
70.creator: Mark Osborne and John Stevenson
70.why: The secret scroll that every fighter wants turns out to be blank and shows only the reader's face. The answer is very easy to know, and the proud student cannot accept it. The clumsy panda can. The film shows the passage's opening pair in a comedy.

71.title: Rashomon
71.creator: Akira Kurosawa
71.why: Four people tell the story of one death, and each account is confident and different. The men who listen at the gate must admit that they do not know what happened. The film makes the viewer practise the passage's first line: to know not-knowing.

71.title: Doubt
71.creator: John Patrick Shanley
71.why: A nun is certain that a priest has done wrong, and she acts on her certainty without proof. In the last scene she admits her doubts and weeps. The film shows the passage's sickness, which is not knowing that one does not know, and the moment the sickness is seen as a sickness.

71.title: Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure
71.creator: Stephen Herek
71.why: Two cheerful students who know very little meet Socrates and repeat to him his own idea that wisdom is to know that you know nothing. They agree that this describes them. The joke is that the two fools already have the passage's highest state, and the experts in the film do not.

71.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
71.creator: Douglas Adams
71.why: A great computer calculates the answer to everything, and the answer is a number that means nothing, because nobody knew what the question was. Adams makes comedy from people who do not know that they do not know. That is the passage's sickness.

71.title: Titanic
71.creator: James Cameron
71.why: The owners and officers are sure that the ship cannot sink, so they carry too few lifeboats and keep up speed among ice. Their certainty is the disaster. The film shows the passage's second line: not to know that one does not know is a sickness.

71.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
71.creator: Daniel Kahneman
71.why: Kahneman reports decades of experiments on overconfidence. People feel sure when they have little evidence, and experts do this too. His remedy is to learn the pattern of the error. The book gives modern evidence for the passage: the one who treats the sickness as a sickness is free of it.

72.title: Do the Right Thing
72.creator: Spike Lee
72.why: On the hottest day of summer a Brooklyn block is cramped, policed, and pressed. Small insults build up. When the police kill a young man, the people's fear ends and the street burns. The film shows the passage's opening: when the people stop fearing, the great dread arrives.

72.title: V for Vendetta
72.creator: James McTeigue; written by the Wachowskis, from the comic by Alan Moore and David Lloyd
72.why: A government watches every home and presses on every life. It rules by fear until the day the crowds are no longer afraid, and then it falls in a night. The film shows the passage's sequence from pressing to loathing to the end of fear.

72.title: Andor
72.creator: Tony Gilroy
72.why: The Empire tightens its hold on towns, prisons, and wages. Each new pressure makes more rebels, and one character says plainly that this is the plan. The series shows a rule that cramps where people dwell, and people who lose their fear as a result.

72.title: The Hunger Games
72.creator: Suzanne Collins
72.why: The Capitol keeps the districts hungry and shows its own importance in a yearly spectacle. The rule holds while people are afraid. One girl's act shows that fear can run out. The novel shows rulers who do the reverse of the passage's sage, who does not display the self.

72.title: Sixteen Tons
72.creator: Merle Travis
72.why: A coal miner sings that each day of work leaves him older and more in debt to the company store, which owns even his death. The song gives the voice of people whose livelihood is pressed down. The passage tells the ruler not to do this.

73.title: Fargo
73.creator: Joel and Ethan Coen
73.why: A car salesman dares a bold crime, and each bold step kills someone. Police chief Marge Gunderson is unhurried, pregnant, and polite. She does not chase. The facts come to her and nothing gets away. The film shows both halves of the passage: daring that kills, and a slack net that loses nothing.

73.title: Breaking Bad
73.creator: Vince Gilligan
73.why: Walter White finds his courage and uses it to dare more and more. The daring brings killing, as the passage says. For years he seems to escape. The series is built so that every act returns to him in the end, through a wide mesh that loses nothing.

73.title: WarGames
73.creator: John Badham
73.why: A military computer plays out every possible nuclear war and learns that each one ends in loss. It concludes that the only way to win is not to play. The film shows the passage's second kind of courage, the courage of not daring, as the one that keeps people alive.

73.title: Crime and Punishment
73.creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky
73.why: Raskolnikov believes that a bold man may kill. No detective catches him by force. The investigator Porfiry waits and talks, and the crime comes home by its own weight. The novel can be read beside the passage's way of heaven, which does not summon, and things come of themselves.

74.title: Death Note
74.creator: Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata
74.why: A gifted student finds a notebook that kills any person whose name he writes in it. He decides to do the killing that he thinks the world needs. He begins with criminals and ends with anyone in his way. The series shows a man who hews in the great carpenter's place and wounds himself.

74.title: The Green Mile
74.creator: Frank Darabont
74.why: Prison guards carry out executions as their job. They come to see that one condemned man is innocent, and they kill him because the law requires it. The lead guard carries that act for a very long life. The film shows the hand that is hurt by the axe.

74.title: A Short Film About Killing
74.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
74.why: The film shows two killings at the same length and with the same detail: a murder by a young man, and his hanging by the state. It asks the viewer to see no difference in the act. It raises the passage's question about who may take the place of the one in charge of killing.

74.title: The Ballad of Reading Gaol
74.creator: Oscar Wilde
74.why: Wilde wrote the poem after his own imprisonment. It describes the days before a fellow prisoner is hanged and the effect on every man in the jail, including the warders. The poem shows that an execution harms those who perform it and those who watch.

75.title: The Grapes of Wrath
75.creator: John Steinbeck
75.why: Farm families lose their land to banks and go hungry beside orchards where food is destroyed to keep prices high. Steinbeck states the cause as plainly as the passage does. The people starve because of what those above them take.

75.title: Snowpiercer
75.creator: Bong Joon-ho
75.why: The last people on earth live on one train. The front cars eat steak and the rear cars eat blocks of protein. The rear passengers revolt and go forward and accept that most of them will die. The film shows people who take death lightly because those above take so much.

75.title: Robin Hood
75.creator: Wolfgang Reitherman
75.why: In Disney's animal version, Prince John taxes Nottingham until the people are in jail for debt and the church poor box is empty. The people become hard to govern. A children's film shows the passage's first three lines without change.

75.title: Squid Game
75.creator: Hwang Dong-hyuk
75.why: People who are crushed by debt agree to play children's games in which the losers are killed. They are allowed to leave, and most of them return. The series shows the passage's third case: the people take death lightly because life has been made too thin.

75.title: Fortunate Son
75.creator: Creedence Clearwater Revival (John Fogerty)
75.why: The singer says that he was not born into the families who make wars and avoid taxes, and that the cost falls on people like him. The song is a short and angry statement of the passage's cause: those above have their doings, and those below pay.

76.title: Stalker
76.creator: Andrei Tarkovsky
76.why: The Stalker guides two men through a dangerous Zone that punishes force. In a quiet inner speech he says that the newborn and the growing tree are soft and pliant, that the dying are hard, and that hardness and strength keep company with death. The speech closely follows this passage.

76.title: Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
76.creator: Ang Lee
76.why: Two fighters meet on the tops of living bamboo. The master Li Mu Bai stays soft and lets the stems bend under him. His young opponent is stiff; he disarms her with ease, and she drops after the sword into the water below. The scene shows the passage's pair in bodies and plants: the soft and weak take the place above.

76.title: The Remains of the Day
76.creator: Kazuo Ishiguro
76.why: The butler Stevens builds his whole self on a rigid idea of dignity. He does not bend for his dying father or for the woman who loves him. Late in life he sees what the stiffness cost. The novel shows the passage's hard and strong as the company of death in a living man.

76.title: Moby-Dick
76.creator: Herman Melville
76.why: Captain Ahab will not bend from his purpose for the weather, for his crew, or for reason. The ship goes down with him. The one man who survives floats on a coffin and lets the sea carry him. The novel shows the strong tree that meets the axe.

77.title: It's a Wonderful Life
77.creator: Frank Capra
77.why: Mr. Potter takes from people who have little and adds it to his own surplus. George Bailey lends to them and claims no credit. When George has nothing, the town brings what it has to him. The film shows the way of people and the way of heaven in one small town.

77.title: Schindler's List
77.creator: Steven Spielberg
77.why: Oskar Schindler starts as a man who profits from the war. He ends by spending his whole fortune to keep his workers alive, and he grieves that he did not give more. The film shows a rare person who has more than enough and offers it up.

77.title: God Bless the Child
77.creator: Billie Holiday and Arthur Herzog Jr.
77.why: The song observes that people who have much are given more and people who have nothing lose even that. Holiday sings it as a plain fact of life. It is a statement of the passage's way of people, which takes from those who do not have enough.

77.title: Monopoly
77.creator: Parker Brothers; based on Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game
77.why: In this board game the player with the most property collects rent from the others until they have nothing. Lizzie Magie designed its ancestor in 1904 to show that this rule is unjust. Each game is a small model of the way of people in the passage.

78.title: The Pierre Berton Show (Bruce Lee interview)
78.creator: Pierre Berton; Bruce Lee
78.why: In this interview Bruce Lee tells his listeners to be formless like water. Water takes the shape of each cup or bottle, he says, and water can also crash. His advice is the best-known modern statement of the passage's image: nothing is softer than water, and nothing beats it against the hard.

78.title: Gandhi
78.creator: Richard Attenborough
78.why: The film follows Gandhi's campaigns against the British Empire. Unarmed people walk to the sea to make salt and accept blows without striking back. The empire has no answer to this. The film shows the weak overcoming the strong, and how few people can walk that way.

78.title: The Dark Knight
78.creator: Christopher Nolan
78.why: At the end Batman takes the blame for another man's crimes so that the city keeps its hope. He accepts being hunted. The film can be read beside the passage's saying: the one who takes on the dirt of the state is its true lord.

78.title: The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
78.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
78.why: A happy city depends on one child who is kept in filth and bears all its misery. The child did not choose this and gets no honour. Le Guin, who later made her own English version of the Tao Te Ching, shows the dark mirror of the passage: the dirt of the state forced onto the weakest.

79.title: The Banshees of Inisherin
79.creator: Martin McDonagh
79.why: Two friends on a small island fall out. Each attempt to settle the matter leaves more hurt behind, and at the end, on a beach, one offers to call them even and the other refuses to let the grievance end. The film shows the passage's first lines: make peace in a great grievance, and some grievance is left over.

79.title: The Godfather
79.creator: Francis Ford Coppola
79.why: Don Corleone does favours and tells each person that a day may come when he will ask for a service in return. He keeps every tally in order to claim on it. Every peace between the families holds a future killing. The film shows the one without de, who collects.

79.title: Pay It Forward
79.creator: Mimi Leder
79.why: A boy proposes that a person who receives a great favour should not repay it and should help three other people. The giver holds the debt and makes no claim. The film shows the passage's sage with the left tally, the creditor's half that is never presented.

79.title: The Count of Monte Cristo
79.creator: Alexandre Dumas
79.why: Edmond Dantès is wronged and spends years and a fortune to collect on every debt owed to him. He collects, and innocent people are harmed, and he ends in doubt about his right. The novel shows the cost of pressing a claim that is fully just.

79.title: The Gift
79.creator: Lewis Hyde
79.why: Hyde studies cultures in which a gift must keep moving and is not paid back to the giver. He argues that a gift that becomes a claim stops being a gift. The book gives a modern account of the passage's tally that is held and not demanded.

80.title: Walden
80.creator: Henry David Thoreau
80.why: Thoreau lives for two years in a small cabin near a railway that he does not need to ride. He counts how few tools a person needs and finds his plain food good. The book is the classic American version of the passage: tools at hand that go unused.

80.title: Local Hero
80.creator: Bill Forsyth
80.why: An oil company sends a young executive to buy a whole Scottish village. He finds a small place with few people and slow days, and he does not want to leave. The film shows the pull of the passage's small state on a man from the world of boats and carts.

80.title: Witness
80.creator: Peter Weir
80.why: A city detective hides among the Amish, who know about cars, telephones, and guns and choose not to use them. A barn is raised in one day by neighbours with hand tools. The film shows a real community that lives close to the passage's picture.

80.title: Animal Crossing
80.creator: Nintendo (Katsuya Eguchi and Hisashi Nogami)
80.why: The player lives in a small village with a few neighbours. There is nothing to win. The player catches fish, plants flowers, and talks to the neighbours, and the days follow the real calendar. Millions of players choose the passage's life of sweet food and a home at rest.

80.title: Always Coming Home
80.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
80.why: Le Guin imagines the Kesh, a people of small towns in a future California. They have access to advanced machines and mostly leave them alone. Le Guin studied the Tao Te Ching for decades. The novel is a full picture of the passage's small state with few people.

80.title: WALL-E
80.creator: Andrew Stanton
80.why: People have left the earth on a great ship where machines carry them, feed them, and speak for them. They use every tool and have forgotten how to walk. The film shows the opposite of the passage's village, and it ends with people who return to the soil.

81.title: Babette's Feast
81.creator: Gabriel Axel
81.why: A refugee cook wins a lottery and spends all of the money on one dinner for the plain village that took her in. She says afterwards that she is not poor. The film shows the passage's sage, who gives everything to others and has more.

81.title: The Gift of the Magi
81.creator: O. Henry
81.why: A poor husband and wife each sell their one treasure to buy a gift for the other. The gifts are now useless, and the couple are richer than before. The story shows the passage's arithmetic: having given to others, one has more again.

81.title: Think Small (Volkswagen Beetle advertisement)
81.creator: Doyle Dane Bernbach (Helmut Krone and Julian Koenig)
81.why: At a time of large cars and loud claims, this advertisement showed a small car in an empty page and described it in plain, modest sentences. Readers trusted it. It is still an advertisement, but it shows that plain words can win trust where beautiful words do not.

81.title: Mad Men
81.creator: Matthew Weiner
81.why: Don Draper has a gift for beautiful words, and he uses it to sell cigarettes and to hide who he is. The people closest to him learn that they cannot trust what he says. The series is a long study of the passage's second line.

81.title: Thank You for Smoking
81.creator: Jason Reitman
81.why: A tobacco lobbyist can win any argument, and he teaches his son that a person who argues well is never wrong. The film lets the audience enjoy his skill and see that it has no relation to the good. It shows the passage's line on those who argue.

81.title: The Hobbit
81.creator: J. R. R. Tolkien
81.why: The dragon Smaug lies on a heap of gold that he cannot use. The dwarf king who wins the heap falls sick with the wish to keep it all. Bilbo gives away his share to make peace and goes home content. The novel shows the pile and the open hand side by side.
